resources.title: 'Anti-' & 'Auto-'

content.topicNotes: 'Anti-' Means Against Prefixes are letters or words placed at the start of words which change their meaning. The prefix 'anti-' means being against something. Let's look at some examples of words beginning with 'anti'... Anticlockwise (=against= clockwise) Antiseptic (=against= germs) Antibiotic (=against= bacteria) Antisocial (=against= being social) Antisocial Antisocial means not social. 'Auto-' Means Self Prefixes are letters or words placed at the start of words which change their meaning. The prefix 'auto-' means 'self'. Let's look at some examples of words beginning with 'auto'... Autobiography An autobiography is an account you write of your own life. So think of it as a story you write about your=self=. Autograph An autograph is a signature. In other words, your name written by your=self=. Automatic Something that is automatic works by it=self=. For example, an automatic car changes gears by itself. Autonomous A country or place that is autonomous can govern or rule it=self=. Autonomous Cars Autonomous cars can drive themselves. Autograph Signing an autograph is signing your own name.

resources.title: 'Ei', 'Eigh' & 'Ey' Spellings

content.topicNotes: Spelling Words with the 'Ei' Sound Words with the 'ei' sound can either be spelt using 'ei', 'eigh' or 'ey'. Let's look at some examples of words using these spellings... 'Ei' Vein. 'Eigh' Weigh. Neighbour. Eight. Sleigh. 'Ey' They. Obey. Prey. Spelling Words with the 'Ei' Sound Words with the 'ei' sound can either be spelt using 'ei', 'eigh' or 'ey'. Let's look at some examples of words using these spellings... Vein Weigh Sleigh Neighbours Prey

resources.title: 'Mis-', 'Dis-' & 'Re-'

content.topicNotes: 'Dis-' and 'Mis-' Make Words Negative Prefixes are letters or words placed at the start of words which change their meaning. The prefixes ‘__dis-__’ and ‘__mis-__’ give words negative meanings. Let's look at some examples of words beginning with 'dis' and 'mis'... Misunderstood Misunderstood means =not= understood. Disagree To disagree means to =not= agree. Disappear To disappear means to vanish or =no longer= appear. Misspell To misspell means to spell =wrongly=. Dishonest Dishonest means =not= honest. Disappear This man has disappeared. He does =not= appear anymore. Disinterest Boo is disinterested in who wins or loses. Disinterested means being impartial or unbiased. Dishonest Pinocchio's nose grows when he is dishonest. Dishonest means =not= honest. Dislike I hate you means I dislike you. 'Re-' Means Back or Again Prefixes are letters or words placed at the start of words which change their meaning. The prefix ‘__re-__’ means ‘again’ or ‘back’. Let's look at some examples of words beginning with 're'... Recycle To recycle is to use =again=. Refresh To refresh is to make fresh =again=. Return To return is to send =back=. Review To review is to look at =again=. Reverse This video clip is being shown in reverse. The action is happening backwards. Recycling These otters are recycling. We recycle things to use the materials again. Restaurant Review A restaurant review is an assessment of a restaurant.

resources.title: 'Sub-' & 'Super-'

content.topicNotes: 'Sub-' Means Under or Below Prefixes are letters or words placed at the start of words which change their meaning. The prefix 'sub-' means under. Let's look at some words beginning with 'sub'... Submarine A submarine is a ship that goes =under=water. Subheading A subheading is a heading that goes =under= the main heading. Subzero Subzero means =under= the temperature 0. Subway A subway is an =under=ground path. Subteen A subteen is someone younger than a teenager. Subway A subway is a path that goes underground. Substandard Substandard means below what's expected or what's good. 'Super-' Means Above Prefixes are letters or words placed at the start of words which change their meaning. The prefix 'super-' means 'above'. Let's look at some words beginning with 'super'... Superstar A superstar is someone who is more famous than other stars - so '=above=' other stars. Superior Someone or something that is superior is better than or =above= other things. Superjet A superjet is a very large jet - so '=above=' the size of other jets! Superglue Superglue is very strong glue - so '=above=' the strength of other glues! Superman Have you ever wondered why Superman's name begins with super? As you have now learned, super means 'above'. So Superman is 'above' other men in terms of his powers! Supermarket A supermarket is a very large shopping store. Supernatural Aliens are supernatural creatures. Supernatural means going beyond the laws of nature.

resources.title: Accept & Except

content.topicNotes: Accept and Except Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Accept I accept your invitation. To accept means to say yes to something. Except Everyone else is invited except you. Except means apart from. Accept and Except Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. To 'accept' means to say yes to something. 'Except' means apart from. I accept your marriage proposal I like all animals, except for spiders Everyone is happy, except Spongebob Will you accept some money?

resources.title: Across & Through

content.topicNotes: Trans - Across Words beginning with 'trans' generally mean across or beyond something. Transport To transport means to take something across a distance. The noun transport means the movement of things across distances, or vehicles that can move things across distances. Example: What is the best way to =transport= my luggage? Alternative: What is the best way to =move= my luggage? Transform To transform is to change form - to go 'across' forms. Example: At the end of Beauty and the Beast, the beast =transforms= into a prince. Alternative: At the end of Beauty and the Beast, the beast =changes= into a prince. Transfer To transfer is to move something from one place to another - to move something 'across' places. Example: Billie =transferred= £100 into my bank account. Alternative: Billie =sent= £100 across to my bank account. Transcend To transcend is to go beyond something or surpass. Example: Gregory was a romantic - he believed love =transcended= everything else. Alternative: Gregory was a romantic - he believed love =surpassed= everything else. Transnational Transnational means going beyond national boundaries or involving many nations. Example: Poverty is a =transnational= issue. Alternative: Poverty is a =global= issue. Per - Through Words beginning with 'per' generally mean through something. They can also mean something is thoroughly something. Perfect To perfect is to make something as good as it can be or faultless. Think of it as doing something 'thoroughly' until it is or is nearly the best it can be. Example: Johnny trained every day to try and =perfect= his serves. Alternative: Johnny trained every day to try and =make his serves faultless=. Pervade When something like a smell or quality pervades a space, it spreads through it so that it's present everywhere in that space. Example: The smell of Lucinda's perfume =pervaded= the restaurant. Alternative: The smell of Lucinda's perfume =spread throughout= the restaurant. Persevere To persevere is to continue doing something even when you face difficulties. You keep going 'through' the difficulties. Example: The weather conditions were awful, but Matt =persevered= to reach the peak of the mountain he was climbing. Alternative: The weather conditions were awful, but Matt =kept climbing= to reach the peak of the mountain he was climbing. Persist To persist is to keep doing or feeling something, even if it's difficult to do so. The 'sist' part of the word comes from the Latin word for 'to stand', so the word literally means 'stand through' something. Example: The opposition was tough, but the team =persisted= and eventually won. Alternative: The opposition was tough, but the team =kept trying= and eventually won. Per - Through Words beginning with 'per' generally mean through something. They can also mean something is thoroughly something. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'per': Perfect Pervade Persevere Persist

resources.title: Active & Passive Voice
Active & Passive Voice

content.topicNotes: The Active Voice The active voice means the subject of the sentence is doing the action. Let's look at some sentences using the active voice... The dog (subject) ate the food The parrot (subject) flapped its wing The man (subject) shouted The horses (subject) liked to gallop The donkey (subject) sat down The Active Voice The active voice means the subject of the sentence is doing the action. Let's look at some sentences using the active voice... The horse ate the poster The mouse swallowed the cheese The monkey ran away The elf hopped across the road The Passive Voice The passive voice is when the subject of the sentence is having the action done to them. Let's look at some examples of sentences using the passive voice... The goat (subject) is being carried The horse (subject) is being ridden The book (subject) is being read The food (subject) is being eaten The rabbit (subject) is being brushed The Passive Voice The passive voice is when the subject of the sentence is having the action done to them. Let's look at some examples of sentences using the passive voice... The lead is being chased The burgers are being eaten The rabbit was kissed The kitten is being tickled
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Language Techniques

content.topicNotes: The Active Voice The active voice means the subject of the sentence is doing the action. Let's look at some sentences using the active voice. The dog (subject) ate the food The parrot (subject) flapped it's wing The man (subject) shouted The horses (subject) liked to gallop The donkey (subject) sat down

resources.title: Adding a Prefix with a Hyphen

content.topicNotes: Adding a Prefix with a Hyphen: Prefix 'co-' If a prefix ends with a vowel and the root word starts with the same vowel, we can use a hyphen to join them. Prefixes Some examples of prefixes are: 'co-' 're-' 'anti-' 'pro-' Co-operate Prefix: 'co-'(ends in vowel). Word: operate (begins with the same vowel). prefix + word → co-operate Re-evaluate Prefix: 're-' (ends in vowel). Word: evaluate (begins with the same vowel). prefix + word → re-evaluate Anti-inflammatory Prefix: 'anti-' (ends in vowel). Word: inflammatory (begins with the same vowel). prefix + word → anti-inflammatory

resources.title: Adjectives & Adverbs

content.topicNotes: Adjectives & Adverbs You need to know the following key terms: Adjectives Words which describe a noun. They add more information about it. E.g. Gorgeous, disgusting, happy, long, tall, green. Adverbs Words which change verbs, adjectives or other adverbs. They may describe how or when something is done. E.g. Quickly, dangerously, always, never, once, soon, near.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Word Classes

resources.title: Adverbial

content.topicNotes: Adverbials Adverbials include adverbs AND phrases that act like adverbs. Adverbs Adverbs are words that change a verb. E.g. Running slowly - 'slowly' is an adverb because it describes how fast the running is. Adverbs can also change an adjective. E.g. 'really big house' - really' is an adverb because it changed the adjective 'big'. Adverbs as adverbials Adverbs are a type of adverbial. Adverbials tell us information about ‘where, when, why or how’ something happened. E.g. 'Suddenly, he jumped for joy' - the adverb 'suddenly' gives more information about the verb ‘jumped’. Phrases as adverbials E.g. 'Needing to release his joy, he jumped into the sky.' 'Needing to release his joy' adds more information to the verb 'jumped'. 'Needing to release his joy' tells us why the jumping happened. 'Needing to release his joy' is an adverbial. Punctuating adverbials A fronted adverbial is an adverbial at the front of a sentence. Fronted adverbials are always followed by a comma. E.g. 'As the light went out, he burst through the door.' 'As the light went out' is a fronted adverbial.

resources.title: Adverbials
Advice & Advise

content.topicNotes: Advice & Advise Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'advice' and 'advise' are homophones. Advice I received some good advice about what to do. Advice is like guidance. Advice is a noun (a thing). Advise I advise you to stay indoors. To advise someone is to offer guidance or recommendations. Advise is a verb (a doing word).

resources.title: Affect & Effect

content.topicNotes: Affect and Effect Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Affect Did the speaker's ideas affect you? Affect is a verb (a doing word). It means to cause a change in something. Effect The river has an effect on the land. Effect is often used as a noun (a thing). An effect is the result of some kind of change.

resources.title: Aisle & Isle

content.topicNotes: Aisle & Isle Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'aisle' and 'isle' are homophones. Aisle The aisle must be clear for landing. An aisle is a pathway between seats (in a place or train or church). Isle The Isle of Arran is home to Goat Fell. An isle is another word for an island.

resources.title: All & Same

content.topicNotes: Omni - All Words beginning with 'omni' generally mean all or every. Omnipresent Omnipresent literally means present everywhere. It can also be used to mean something has a constant effect everywhere. Example: The Christian God is =omnipresent=. Alternative: The Christian God is =present everywhere, always=. Example: The model was an =omnipresent= fashion icon. Alternative: The model was a =global= fashion icon. Omnipotent Omnipotent means all powerful. Example: Christians believe that God is =omnipotent=. Alternative: Christians believe that God is =all powerful=. Omniscient Omniscient means knowing everything. Example: No human being can be =omniscient=. Alternative: No human being can =know everything=. The Christian God The Christian God is believed to be omnipresent, omnisicent and omnipotent. 'Omni' means all or every, so God is believed to be present everywhere, all knowing and all powerful. Equ - Equal Words beginning with 'equ' generally mean equal. Equal Equal means the same. Example: Jess and Johnny were =equally= competitive. Alternative: Jess and Johnny were =as= competitive as each other. Equation An equation is a maths statement showing that two different values are the same. An equation can also show what happens during a chemical reaction. Example: 2 + 5 = 7 is a mathematical equation. Example: The equation for aerobic respiration is glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Equidistant Equidistant means equally near or far (equal distance). Example: My school is =equidistant= from James' and Jenny's houses. Alternative: My school is the =same distance= from James' and Jenny's houses. Equality Equality means being equal. It's often used in the context of people's rights and status. Example: Everybody in the group wanted =equality=. Alternative: Everybody in the group wanted =everyone to be equal=. Equalise To equalise is to make equal. Example: Many teachers at the school felt overworked, while some felt underworked. The school needed to =equalise= the workload. Alternative: Many teachers at the school felt overworked, while some felt underworked. The school needed to =even= out the workload. Equivalent Things that are equivalent have the same value, purpose, or are of the same amount etc. Example: 1 mile is =equivalent= to 1.6 km. Alternative: 1 mile is =the same= distance as 1.6 km. Equ - Equal Words beginning with 'equ' generally mean equal. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'equ': Equal Equation Equality Equalise Homo - Same Words beginning with 'homo' generally mean being the same as something. Homogeneous Homogeneous means made up of the same kind of parts or people. Example: The ginger children in identical uniforms make up a =homogeneous= group. Alternative: The ginger children in identical uniforms make up a =single-identity= group. Homonym Homonym means words that sound or are spelt the same but have different meanings. Example: Knight and night are =homonyms=. Alternative: Knight and night =sound the same but have different meanings=.

resources.title: Aloud & Allowed

content.topicNotes: Aloud & Allowed Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'aloud' and 'allowed'. Aloud It is important to practice reading aloud. Aloud literally means, 'out loud'. Allowed You are not allowed to run around the pool. If you are allowed to do something, it means that you are permitted.

resources.title: Altar & Alter

content.topicNotes: Altar & Alter Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'altar' and 'alter'. Altar The priest stood up at the altar. An altar is a bit like a table, and you would find it in a church. Alter We need to alter the measurements to make sure that it fits. To alter means to adjust or to change it.

resources.title: Answer Retrieval Questions

content.topicNotes: Answering Retrieval Questions Retrieval questions need you to get information directly from the text. You should NOT use information in your head to answer retrieval questions. Answering retrieval questions To answer retrieval questions, look for the answers in the text. You should NOT answer retrieval questions with information in your head! The information we need does NOT come from our general knowledge or imagination. The information comes from what the text tells us. Highlight the answer To be sure we have the right information, find the part in the text with the answer. Then we should highlight the part of the text that gives us the answer. Example: text According to the text below, why are fish popular pets? Fish are very popular pets because they do not require much attention and they can be left at home alone. Example: answer We can highlight the information, and write the exact words as our answer. Fish are very popular pets because they do not require much attention, and they can be left at home alone. You might think people buy fish because they're cheap and look nice... But this is not written in the text, so it cannot be your answer!
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Comprehension

resources.title: Answering Inference Questions

content.topicNotes: Answering Inference Questions How to answer inference questions? First, you need to search for clues or evidence in the text. You then need to highlight the clues. Finally, you explain what the clue tells us. Thoughts, feelings and motives You can often find clues about a character’s thoughts, feelings or motives. You will find clues about a character’s thoughts, feelings or motives in the author’s descriptions. Where can you find clues? Look out for clues in the descriptions of the character's actions, words, appearance or body language. Example: sentence The child jumped up and down, grinning from ear to ear. The author has not told us how the child feels. Inference The child =jumped up and down=, =grinning= from ear to ear. We can infer the child is happy and excited from the clues we have highlighted. Another Inference Example Sentence The man stared longingly out of the window. Today was so hot that his shirt clung to him uncomfortably. The author has not told us that the man wants to go outside. Inference The man =stared longingly out of the window=. Today was so =hot= that his shirt clung to him =uncomfortably=. We can infer the man wants to go outside from the clues we have highlighted.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Comprehension

resources.title: Answering Summary Questions

content.topicNotes: Answering Summary Questions Summarising is when we explain what a text is about. Summaries We write a summary in our own words, outlining the main idea, without all the details. A summary will be much shorter than the text it describes. Think of a summary as a subtitle for the bit of text it is summarising. Example: text A panda is a type of bear that lives in bamboo forests in the mountains of China. They very occasionally eat other animals, but their diet mainly consists of bamboo. They need to eat a lot of it, and it is not unusual for them to spend 12 hours a day eating. Pandas grow to around 1.5 metres tall, but when they are born they could fit in your hand. Example: summary This paragraph could be summarised as 'Information about pandas'. Summarise To Make Links Summarising is when we explain what a text is about. Summarise to make links Summarising helps us make links. Summarising can connect different paragraphs in a text. Summarising can also link different verses in a poem. Summarising can even connect different texts. Making comparisons Imagine we had another text, summarised as 'Information about giraffes'. Then, we could draw some comparisons to the text summarised as 'Information about pandas': Both texts provide information about animals. Both texts are non-fiction. The texts are about different animals.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Comprehension

resources.title: Apart & Together

content.topicNotes: Co - Together Words beginning with 'co' generally express the idea of togetherness. Connect To connect means to join together. A connection is when two or more things have an association. Example: Lukas and his girlfriend have a strong =connection=. Alternative: Lukas and his girlfriend have a strong =bond=. Collide When things collide, they bang together. Example: Only the driver was injured when the police car =collided= with the getaway truck. Alternative: Only the driver was injured when the police car =crashed= into the getaway truck. Co-exist To co-exist means to exist together (at the same time). Example: Some people think religion and science cannot =co-exist=. Alternative: Some people think religion and science cannot =exist at the same time=. Coincidence A coincidence is when two similar things happen unintentionally - they happen 'together' by chance. Example: It was a =coincidence= that John and Paul ran into each other at Sainsbury's - they hadn't planned to meet! Alternative: It was =by chance= that John and Paul ran into each other at Sainsbury's - they hadn't planned to meet! Collect To collect means to bring together. A collection is a group of things, and a collector is someone who brings things together. Example: Ben was a keen =collector= of football stickers. Alternative: Ben was a keen =gatherer= of football stickers. Example: Matthew had an impressive =collection= of vinyl. Alternative: Matthew had an impressive =set= of vinyl. Example: Jess =collected= her children from school at 4pm.Alternative: Jess =picked up= her children from school at 4pm. Co - With Words beginning with 'co' generally mean with something or together. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'co': Connect Collide Co-exist Coincidence Collect Ex - Out Of Words beginning with 'ex' generally mean being out of something. Exclude To exclude means to leave out. Example: Jono was =excluded= from the football team. Alternative: Jono was =left out= of the football team. Extend To extend means to make something larger, longer, bigger etc. Think of something growing outwards. It also means to stretch out or offer out. Example: My parents are =extending= our kitchen. Alternative: My parents are =increasing the length= of our kitchen. Example: In the past, war leaders would =extend= olive branches as peace offerings. Alternative: In the past, war leaders would =offer= olive branches as peace offerings. Exogenous If something is exogenous, it comes from outside of something. It's caused by external factors. resources.title: Ascent & Assent

content.topicNotes: Ascent & Assent Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'ascent' and 'assent'. Ascent The ascent was dangerous due to unstable rocks. To ascend something is to go up it (e.g. a mountain, or an escalator) Assent The prime minister assented to the policy change. To assent means to agree or approve something.

resources.title: Autobiographical Text

content.topicNotes: Autobiographical Text An autobiography is a text written in the first person about a person’s life. Autobiography Autobiographical texts often span decades. Autobiographical texts describe the most important events in the person’s life. Autobiography also includes a person's thoughts and feelings. Autobiographies & biographies Autobiographies and biographies have some similarities as well as differences. Autobiographies and biographies are about one person’s life and describe key events of this person’s life in the past tense. A biography is written about someone else’s life. An autobiography is about the writer’s life. Famous autobiographies Many famous people have written and published autobiographies, including actors, politicians and musicians. Sometimes autobiographies are also called ‘memoirs’. Memoirs are often written to inspire and motivate the reader. Memoirs also provide factual information about a person’s life. 'Becoming’ by Michelle Obama One famous autobiography is called ‘Becoming’ by Michelle Obama. Michelle Obama was the previous First Lady when her husband Barack Obama was President. Michelle Obama's autobiography Michelle Obama's autobiography gives details about her and her family’s time in the White House during his presidency. Michelle Obama's autobiography also describes her life before this during her childhood.

resources.title: Avoiding Ambiguity in Writing

content.topicNotes: Avoiding Ambiguity in Writing Ambiguity is when something can be understood in many different ways. The key to avoiding ambiguity in your writing is to plan your writing. Planning your writing can be done on 3 levels: Whole response level You need to plan what you will write so that your response has a structure that can be followed easily. It is good to have each point from your plan in its own paragraph. An easy to follow structure will help you to develop your points one at a time. An easy to follow structure helps the reader track your discussion and consider each point one at a time. Sentence level Avoiding ambiguity in a sentence involves making sure the sentence doesn't get too complicated. You can use punctuation to break up complicated sentences to make sentences easier to understand. Complex sentences A complex sentence contains a main clause as well as a subordinate clause. You may be able to use multiple subordinate clauses in a sentence if you are a strong writer. But if you are not so confident, it is wise to only use 1 or 2 subordinate clauses at most. It is better to use shorter sentences to avoid ambiguity. Word level The right word choice is very important to avoid ambiguity in your writing. Some things you need to think about are: Using appropriate adjectives and adverbs to add detail. Keep a dictionary and a thesaurus handy to expand your vocabulary. Experiment with vocabulary and pay attention to the feedback if you happen to use it incorrectly. Using Appropriate Words to Avoid Ambiguity Using appropriate adjectives and adverbs to add detail to your writing. There are a few tools you can use to help you use the correct adjectives and adverbs: Use a thesaurus Use a dictionary Experiment with vocabulary and listen to feedback

resources.title: Away & Far

content.topicNotes: Ab - Away From Words beginning with 'ab' generally mean being away from something. Abnormal To be abnormal means to be 'away from' what is normal. In other words, to be different from what is normal. Example: That jacket is an =abnormal= colour. Alternative: That jacket is an =unusual= colour. Absent To be absent means to be away. Example: James was =absent= from school today. Alternative: James was =not at= school today. Abbreviate To abbreviate is to shorten something, especially words. Example: As soon as possible =abbreviates= to ASAP. Alternative: As soon as possible =shortens= to ASAP. Abstain To abstain is to stay away from doing something - in other words, to stop doing something. Example: Bertie thought it was a good idea to =abstain= from drinking. Alternative: Bertie thought it was a good idea to =stay away= from drinking. Abject Abject means really bad, really unhappy, really hopeless etc. The word abject is used to stress how bad something is. Example: William lived in =abject= poverty. Alternative: William lived in =utter= poverty. Ab - Away From Words beginning with 'ab' generally mean being away from something. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'ab': Abnormal Absent Abbreviate Abstain Abject Ab Example - Abnormal To be abnormal means to be different from what is normal. Dogs don't tend to wear tuxes or dance like this. So this dog is acting abnormally. Tele - Far Words beginning with 'tele' generally mean far or far off. Telescope A telescope is a device that makes far-off objects seem closer. Example: Kevin used his telescope to look at stars. Telephone A telephone is a device that can transmit voices over far distances. So you can talk to people in far off places using a telephone! Example: I haven't seen Jenny in three months, but we speak every day on the telephone. Television A television is a device that transmits visual images to be displayed on screens elsewhere. So a television allows you to see far off things from where you are! Example: Gareth has never seen a meerkat in real life, but he has seen plenty on the television. Teleport To teleport means to transfer something across a very far distance instantly. It's often used in a sci-fi context to mean to transfer across space. Example: It would be so great to =teleport= to school when it's raining so that I wouldn't get wet walking to the bus stop. Alternative: It would be so great to =be instantly transported= to school when it's raining so that I wouldn't get wet walking to the bus stop. Tele - Far Words beginning with 'tele' generally mean far or far off. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'tele': Telescope Telephone Television Teleport

resources.title: Back & Down

content.topicNotes: Re - Back Words beginning with 're' generally mean going back or again. Redo To redo is to do again. Example: James' homework was so bad that he had to =redo= it. Alternative: James' homework was so bad that he had to =do it again=. Recognise To recognise is to know something because you've seen it before. Example: Polly looked so different with blonde hair that people struggled to =recognise= her. Alternative: Polly looked so different with blonde hair that people struggled to =identify= her. React A react is to respond to something (act again). Example: Helena =reacted= to the mean comments by crying. Alternative: Helena =responded= to the mean comments by crying. Review To review is to look at something again. Example: Lenny was spending money so fast he had to =review= his finances. Alternative: Lenny was spending money so fast he had to =look over= his finances. Renegotiate To renegotiate is to discuss something again. Example: Martha didn't like her current salary so asked to =renegotiate= it with her boss. Alternative: Martha didn't like her current salary so asked to =discuss it again= with her boss. De - Down Words beginning with 'de' generally mean going down or away. Decelerate To decelerate means to slow down. Example: The car =decelerated= to 30 mph. Alternative: The car =slowed= to 30 mph. Dethrone To dethrone means to remove from power. Example: Duncan III was =dethroned= by his nephew Duncan II. Alternative: Duncan III was =removed from power= by his nephew Duncan II. Decelerating Words beginning with 'de' generally mean going down or away. This mouse is going so fast that he flies off. He slows down when he flies off - he decelerates.

resources.title: Ball & Bawl

content.topicNotes: Ball and Bawl Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Ball I kicked a ball. A ball is a round object. Bawl I hurt myself, which made me bawl my eyes out. To bawl is to cry. Homophones Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Bawl (to cry) Ball (round object) Balls! A ball is a round object. Do not confuse the word 'ball' with the word 'bawl', which sounds the same but means to cry. Let's look at some different types of balls... Tennis ball Beach ball Golf ball Rugby ball

resources.title: Before & After

content.topicNotes: Pre - Before Words beginning with 'pre' generally mean before something. Prefix A prefix is a group of letters or word at the start of a word - 'before' the word has begun. Example: The =prefix= 'pre' means before. Alternative: The =foreword= 'pre' means before. Present To be present is to be there - to be 'before' someone or something. Example: Andre was always =present= at football matches. Alternative: Andre was always =at= football matches. Prepare To prepare is to get something ready beforehand. Example: Katie =prepared= her outfit hours before the party started. Alternative: Katie =got her outfit ready= hours before the party started. Premise A premise is an initial idea that other actions or ideas come from. The premise comes 'before' the new ideas or actions. Example: He accepted the job on the =premise= that he would get a pay rise within three months. Alternative: He accepted the job =with the knowledge= that he would get a pay rise within three months. Preparation To prepare is to get ready 'beforehand'. Examples of preparation are: Preparing food (for a meal) Preparing an outfit (for an event) Preparing for an exam Post - After Words beginning with 'post' generally mean after something. Postpone To postpone means to put off until later or until after something else. Example: Sally had to =postpone= her driving test because she fell ill. Alternative: Sally had to =delay= her driving test because she fell ill. Postgraduate Postgraduate refers to a course studied after completing a first degree. Example: Penelope is a =postgraduate= student at the University of Exeter. Alternative: Penelope is a =Master's= student at the University of Exeter. Postscript A postscript is something written at the end of a letter. It's often written in the abbreviated form 'P.S.' A postscript is also an additional bit of information that's added after an event's over. Example: A =postscript= to the story is that the boys ended up living together eventually. Alternative: A =development= of the story is that the boys ended up living together eventually. Postmortem A post-mortem is a medical examination of a dead body - so an examination 'after' someone has died. Example: The doctor needed to carry out a =post-mortem=. Alternative: The doctor needed to carry out an =examination on the dead body=. Postnatal Postnatal means the period of time after a baby is born. Example: The mother needed =postnatal= care. Alternative: The mother needed =care after= her baby was born.

resources.title: Belief & Study

content.topicNotes: Ism - Belief Words ending in 'ism' generally refer to a belief or doctrine. Communism Communism is the belief in a society where the state owns all industry and there are no social classes. Example: Fear of communism was very high around the time of the Vietnam War. Scepticism Scepticism is the belief that something isn't true. Example: The company's claim that it recycled all used paper was met with =scepticism=. Alternative: The company's claim that it recycled all used paper was met with =doubt=. Capitalism Capitalism is a political and economic system in which private owners own industry, not the state. Example: In the play An Inspector Calls, Mr Birling represents the evils of capitalism. Hedonism Hedonism is the theory that the most important thing in life is seeking pleasure. Example: Sacha quit her job to pursue a life of =hedonism=. Alternative: Sacha quit her job to pursue a life of =seeking pleasure=. Logy - Study Words ending in 'logy' generally mean the study or science of something. Biology Biology is the study of living organisms. Theology Theology is the study of religion. Sociology Sociology is the study of societies. Psychology Psychology is the study of the human mind. Technology Technology is using science for practical purposes. Logy - Study Words ending in 'logy' generally mean the study or science of something. Here are some examples of words ending with the suffix 'logy': Biology Theology Sociology Psychology Technology

resources.title: Believing & Thinking

content.topicNotes: Cred Words containing 'cred' generally relate to believing. Credible If something is credible, it is believable or trustworthy. Example: You should only use =credible= sources for your assignment. Alternative: You should only use =trustworthy= sources for your assignment. Incredible Something that's incredible is unbelievable. Example: The view from our hotel room was just =incredible=. Alternative: The view from our hotel room was =unbelievable=. Incredulous Someone who is incredulous can't believe something. Example: Molly was =incredulous= that Georgia was late for her exam. Alternative: Molly =could not believe= that Georgia was late for her exam. Credibly Something done credibly is done in a believable way. Example: The journalists reported =credibly= on the events of the Watergate scandal. Alternative: The journalists reported =trustworthily= on the events of the Watergate scandal. The Incredibles The Incredibles is a film about an incredible family. The family are incredible because they have superpowers - their powers aren't believable. Put - Think Words containing 'put' generally express the idea of thinking. Computer A computer is a 'thinking' machine. Computers store and organise information and carry out calculations, like a brain. Example: All Hugo wanted was a new computer for Christmas. Dispute To dispute is to question what someone thinks. Example: Jack =disputed= the claim that Spain is the best holiday destination. Alternative: Jack =disagreed with= the claim that Spain is the best holiday destination. Input To input is to contribute your thoughts. Example: Florence used her knowledge of animals to =input= into the discussion. Alternative: Florence used her knowledge of animals to =contribute= to the discussion. Put - Think Words containing 'put' generally express the idea of thinking. Here are some examples of words containing the root word 'put': Computer Dispute Input

resources.title: Berry & Bury

content.topicNotes: Berry and Bury Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Berry I ate a berry. A berry is a type of fruit. Bury I had to bury treasure. To bury is to put underground. Berries! A berry is a type of fruit. Do not confuse the word berry with the word bury, which means to put underground. Let's look at some common berries... Strawberry Raspberry Blueberry Blackberry Mary Berry Mary Berry is a famous food writer. You might have seen her on the TV show Bake Off. Her surname sounds like the word 'bury', which means to put underground, but is spelt differently. This is because berry and bury are homophones!

resources.title: Brackets

content.topicNotes: Using Brackets for Parenthesis We use parenthesis to add extra information to a sentence. Let's look at how we can use brackets for parenthesis... Wolf in the woods The wolf (which lived in the woods) liked the howl. Jimmy The man (whose name was Jimmy) was wearing a stripey t-shirt. Angry man The man (who could not fix his computer) was angry. Delicious meal The meal (which was delicious) was eaten quickly. Scared girl The girl (who was afraid of heights) did not want to go in the air balloon. Using Brackets for Parenthesis You have already learned that we can use brackets to add extra information to sentences. Let's look at some examples... Famous pop star Selina Gomez (who is a famous pop star) is my friend. Beautiful horse The horse (which is very beautiful) is watching the sunset. Dancing sheep The sheep (which loves to dance) is called Shaun.

resources.title: Brake & Break

content.topicNotes: Brake and Break Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Brake Use the brake on your bike. A brake is something to help you slow down. Break Don't break the vase! To break means to separate something into pieces. It can also mean to stop something from working properly.

resources.title: Bridal & Bridle

content.topicNotes: Bridal & Bridle Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'bridal' and 'bridle'. Bridal Bridal shoes are very expensive. Bridal means something related to a wedding bride. Bridle He attached the bridle securely onto the horse before the race. A bridle is the headgear that goes on a horse.

resources.title: Building Cohesion in Writing

content.topicNotes: Building Cohesion in Writing The reader can process a written discussion better if you create a cohesive piece of writing. A cohesive piece of writing can be easily followed. Whole text cohesion There are some simple signposts that we can use to control the way the reader reads our discussion. When presenting points in a discussion for non-fiction writing, we can separate them by saying ‘firstly’, then ‘secondly’, then ‘thirdly’, then ‘finally’. ‘Firstly’, then ‘secondly’, then ‘thirdly’, then ‘finally’ should be the point where you introduce a new paragraph. Paragraph cohesion You can still signpost a slight or substantial change in direction within a paragraph. Words like ‘however’, ‘although’ or ‘nevertheless’ can suggest that there’s an alternative to the point just discussed. Words like ‘then’ and ‘when’ suggest the next stage of your argument. Sentence cohesion Subordinating conjunctions can be used to build cohesion in writing. Subordinating conjunctions help link a main clause to a subordinate clause. Subordinating conjunctions can also provide key information about the link. 'However', 'then', 'because' and 'if' are examples of subordinating conjunctions. Building Cohesion in Argumentative Writing The reader can process a written discussion better if you create a cohesive piece of writing. A cohesive piece of writing can be easily followed. Argumentative writing Indications of contrast are very effective in argumentative writing. Words like 'however', 'although' and 'nonetheless' are indications of contrast. Indications of contrast example ‘I see your point about mobile phones allowing you to access information in class, =however=, the amount of distraction they cause makes them a bad thing for a classroom environment.’ The word 'however' introduces a contrast to the main clause and signposts the reader that there’s an alternative point of view.

resources.title: Bullet Points: Capital Letters

content.topicNotes: Using Capital Letters in Bullet Points There are different ways we can begin bullet points. One way is by starting with a capital letter. Another way is by not starting with a capital letter. With a capital letter This bullet point starts with a capital letter. Without a capital letter this bullet point does not start with a capital letter.

resources.title: Bullet Points: Consistency

content.topicNotes: Import Rule for Using Bullet Points When you use bullet points, you must use the same rule for all bullet points. Capital letters If one bullet point starts with a capital letter, all bullet points must start with a capital letter. No capital letters If one bullet point starts with a lower case letter (a small letter), all bullet points must start with a lower case letter. Punctuation If one bullet point ends with punctuation, all bullet points must end with punctuation. No punctuation If one bullet ends with no punctuation, all bullet points must end with no punctuation.

resources.title: Bullet Points: Puctuation

content.topicNotes: Ways of Ending Bullet Points There are different ways we can end bullet points. One way is by using punctuation at the end, and another way is by not using punctuation at the end of the bullet point. Ending with punctuation This bullet point finishes in a full stop. This bullet point finishes in an exclamation mark! This bullet point finishes with a question mark? Ending without punctuation This bullet point does not finish with punctuation Neither does this bullet point

resources.title: Can

content.topicNotes: Can Modal verbs are verbs that affect other verbs in sentences. 'Can' is a modal verb. Can 'Can' means you are able to do something. Examples I can dance. You can go to the cinema. He can write. She can feed the dog.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Modal Verbs

resources.title: Capable & Relating

content.topicNotes: Ble - Capable Words ending in 'ble' generally mean something is capable of being that way. Edible If something is edible, it's able to be eaten. Example: The soup was past its sell-by date, but it was still =edible=. Alternative: The soup was past its sell-by date, but you =could still eat= it. Disposable If something's disposable, it can be thrown away. Example: Do you prefer using =disposable= razors, or ones with replaceable heads? Alternative: Do you prefer using razors you =can throw away=, or ones with replaceable heads? Lovable If something is lovable, it's capable of being loved. Example: Shaggy was such a =lovable= dog. Alternative: Shaggy was such a =wonderful= dog. Measurable If something is measurable, you can measure it. Example: A pencil is =measurable=; emotions are not. Alternative: A pencil =can be measured=; emotions cannot. Excitable If something is excitable, it gets excited. Example: Harold was very =excitable= around new people. Alternative: Harold often got very =excited= around new people. Ble - Capable Words ending in 'ble' generally mean something is capable of being that way. Here are some examples of words that end in the suffix 'ble': Edible Disposable Lovable Measurable Excitable Al - Relating To Words ending in 'al' often mean relating to something. Regional Regional means relating to the region. Example: In 2018, Italy held =regional= elections. Alternative: In 2018, Italy held elections for =different regions=. Coastal Coastal means relating to the coast. Example: Blackpool is a =coastal= city. Alternative: Blackpool is a city =on the coast=. Controversial Controversial means relating to public disagreement (controversy). Example: Roger has made some =controversial= statements about women in the past. Alternative: Roger has made some =contestable= statements about women in the past. Skeletal Skeletal means relating to a skeleton. Example: Suzie was =skeletally= thin. Alternative: Suzie looked =like a skeleton= she was so thin. Professional Professional means relating to work (a profession). Example: Sammy had three years of =professional= experience. Alternative: Sammy had three years' =work= experience. Traditional Traditional means relating to tradition or an aspect of tradition. Example: Ruby was determined not to be a =traditional= housewife. Alternative: Ruby was determined not to be a =usual= housewife.

resources.title: Capital Letters

content.topicNotes: Capital Letters Capital letters are used for four reasons: To begin a sentence Capital letters are used at the beginning of every sentence. For proper nouns Proper nouns are the names of people, places, cities or organisations. 'London' is a proper noun and should always start with a capital letter. The word 'river' is NOT a proper noun so should start with a lower case letter. The name 'River Thames' should start with capital letters because it is the name of a river. To write the pronoun ‘I’ Whenever we write the pronoun ‘I’ it must be a capital letter. There are no exceptions to this. For example: ‘It is a shame that i can’t swim.’ ❌ ‘It is a shame that I can’t swim.’ ✅ In titles The following words should start with a capital letter in a title" The first word in the title. The last word in the title. All the important words in a title (e.g. NOT 'a', 'an', 'the', 'and', 'with', etc.) Capital Letters Here are some examples of using capital letters correctly. Bowling is a sport I enjoy Sentences always start with a capital letter. 'I' is always written with a capital letter. London is a city in England Sentences always start with a capital letter. 'London' and 'England' start with a capital letter because they are proper nouns. Manchester United is not a team I enjoy watching Sentences always start with a capital letter. 'Manchester United' starts with capital letters because it is a proper noun. 'I' is always written with a capital letter. This cat is called Bruce Sentences always start with a capital letter. 'Bruce' starts with capital letters because it is a proper noun.

resources.title: Carrying & Leading

content.topicNotes: Duc - Lead Words containing 'duc' generally mean leading. Conduct In the musical sense, to conduct means to lead a group of musicians in the music they're playing. Example: He =conducted= the piece beautifully. Alternative: He =led= [the orchestra through] the piece beautifully. Educate To educate means to lead people to greater knowledge. Example: She =educated= me on the civil rights movement in America. Alternative: She =taught= me about the civil rights movement in America. Duc - Lead Words containing 'duc' generally mean leading. Here are some examples of words containing the root 'duc': Conduct Educate Port - Carry Words containing 'port' generally mean carrying. Portable Things that are portable can be carried. Example: I really need a =portable= fan in this heat. Alternative: I really need a =handheld= fan in this heat. Porter A porter is someone whose job it is to carry luggage. Example: My suitcase was so heavy that even the porter struggled to carry it. Export To export is to send or carry things from one place to another. It's often used in the context of taking things from your country to another country. Example: The strawberries were =exported= to other European countries. Alternative: The strawberries were =sent to= other European countries. Import To import is to send or carry things into somewhere from somewhere else. It's often used in the context of bringing things from one country to your own country. Example: The car was =imported= from Germany. Alternative: The car was =sent= over =from= Germany. Report To report is to describe something. Someone who is reporting is 'carrying' back information about something. A report is a document detailing this kind of information. It's a written account of the information 'carried' back. Example: Ingrid =reported= the event with total accuracy. Alternative: Ingrid =recounted= the event with total accuracy.

resources.title: Cereal & Serial

content.topicNotes: Cereal & Serial Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'cereal' and 'serial'. Cereal Some cereal brands add too much sugar to their products. Cereals are types of grain, commonly made into breakfast cereal. Serial There is a new two-part drama serial on the television. Serial describes something that is repeated.

resources.title: Certainty & Clarity

content.topicNotes: Cert - Certainty Words containing 'cert' generally involve the idea of certainty or surety. Certain If something is certain, it's definitely true or you're absolutely sure of it. Example: Matt was =certain= he had lost his wallet in the restaurant. Alternative: Matt was =sure= he had lost his wallet in the restaurant. Ascertain To ascertain mean to find out something for certain. Example: Ellen used scales to =ascertain= the weight. Alternative: Ellen used scales to =find out= the exact weight. Certify To certify something means to confirm that it's true or valid. Example: You must =certify= the document before it goes to court. Alternative: You must =validate= the document before it goes to court. Clar - Clear Words containing 'clar' generally mean being clear. Declare To declare means to say something clearly. Example: The leader =declared= war on the enemies. Alternative: The leader =announced= war on the enemies. Clarify To clarify means to make clear. Example: Can you =clarify= what you meant by that comment? Alternative: Can you =make clear= what you meant by that comment? Clarification Clarification is an explanation that makes something clearer or easier to understand. Example: George asked for =clarification= about his job role. Alternative: George asked for a =clear explanation= of his job role.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Common Word Roots

resources.title: Characterised By

content.topicNotes: Ous - Characterised By Words ending in 'ous' generally mean characterised by or full of. Nutritious Nutritious means full of nutrition. In other words, very nourishing. Example: Broccoli and carrots are very =nutritious= foods. Alternative: Broccoli and carrots and very =nourishing= foods. Studious Studious means characterised by studying a lot. Example: Emmy was a very =studious= girl at school. Alternative: Emmy =loved studying= at school. Adventurous Adventurous means characterised by adventure. Example: Damien was known for being very =adventurous=. Alternative: Damien was known for =loving adventure=. Disastrous Disastrous means characterised by disaster. Example: The school trip was =disastrous= from start to finish. Alternative: The school trip was =full of disaster= from start of finish. Famous Someone or something that's famous is characterised by having a lot of fame. Example: Justin Bieber is a very =famous= pop star. Alternative: Justin Bieber is a very =well known= pop star. Ous - Characterised By Words ending in 'ous' generally mean characterised by or full of. Here are some examples of words with the suffix 'ous': Nutritious Studious Adventurous Disastrous Famous Y - Characterised By Words ending in 'y' generally mean something is characterised by or full of something. Tasty Characterised by taste. Example: The bacon sandwich was so =tasty= I ordered another. Alternative: The bacon sandwich was so =full of flavour= I ordered another one. Greasy Characterised by grease. Example: Ruben had not washed his hair in a week - it was so =greasy=. Alternative: Ruben had not washed his hair in a week - it was =covered in grease=. Hazy Characterised by haze. Example: Beijing is often very =hazy= from pollution. Alternative: Beijing is often =covered in a haze= from pollution. Smelly Characterised by smell. Example: Jack was so =smelly=, his scent filled the room when he entered. Alternative: Jack =smelt so strongly=, his scent filled the room when he entered. Juicy Full of juice. Example: The orange juice from Sainsbury's is particularly =juicy=. Alternative: The orange juice from Sainsbury's is particularly =fruity=. Y - Characterised By Words ending in 'y' generally mean something is characterised by or full of something. Here are some examples of words ending in the suffix 'y': Tasty Greasy Hazy Smelly Juicy Ful - Notable For Words ending in 'ful' generally being notable for something. Woeful Woeful means full of sadness or notable for sadness. Example: Grace had a very =woeful= expression. Alternative: Grace had a very =sad= expression. Beautiful Beautiful means notable for looking nice or beauty. Example: Karen was known for being the most =beautiful= girl in town. Alternative: Karen was known for being the most =attractive= girl in town. Powerful Powerful means having lots of power or being notable for having power. Example: Love is a =powerful= force. Alternative: Love is a =strong= force. Peaceful Peaceful means without violence or being notable for being calm. Example: The civil rights movement was characterised by =peaceful= protest. Alternative: The civil rights movement was characterised by =non-violent= protest. Faithful Faithful means being very loyal or being notable for being trustworthy. Example: Ricky calls me whenever I am sad - he is such a =faithful= friend. Alternative: Ricky calls me whenever I am sad - he is such a =loyal= friend. Ful - Notable For Words ending in 'ful' generally being notable for something. Here are some examples of words that end in the suffix 'ful': Woeful Beautiful Powerful Peaceful Faithful

resources.title: Clauses: Using Colons to Separate Clauses

content.topicNotes: Using Colons to Separate Clauses We don’t always need to use a full stop to separate main clauses. Sometimes, we can use other symbols, like a colon (:). Colons We don’t always need to use a full stop to separate main clauses. We can use other symbols, like colons. A colon is a punctuation mark that looks like this: : As you can see, it is one point on top of another. Examples The clock was ticking: midnight was approaching. The dog was sad: he lost his bone. The boy was hungry: he skipped breakfast. Our teacher was angry: the classroom was messy.

resources.title: Clauses: Using Dashes to Separate Clauses

content.topicNotes: Using Dashes to Separate Clauses We don’t always need to use a full stop to separate main clauses. Sometimes, we can use other symbols, like a dash (—). Dashes We don’t always need to use a full stop to separate main clauses. We can use other symbols, like dashes. A dash is a punctuation mark that looks like this: — Examples The man was strong — he never stopped doing exercise. Jerry is funny — I wish he told me a joke. Patricia likes cats — we will get her one for her birthday. More examples Molly finds sums tricky — she needs a little more practice. Will adores animals — he is a vegetarian

resources.title: Clauses: Using Semi-Colons to Separate Clauses

content.topicNotes: Using Semi-Colons to Separate Clauses We don’t always need to use a full stop to separate main clauses. Sometimes, we can use other symbols, like a semi-colon (;). Semi-colons We don’t always need to use a full stop to separate main clauses. We can use other symbols, like semi-colons. A colon is a punctuation mark that looks like this: ; As you can see, it is one point on top of a comma. Examples My boss is angry; I am late again. It is cold; I hope it snows. We are hungry; our lunch was tiny! I am so excited; I go on holiday next week.

resources.title: Climbing & Going

content.topicNotes: Cede - Go Words containing the stems 'cede', 'ceed' or 'cess' generally mean going. Exceed To exceed means to go too far or go beyond something. Example: Simon often =exceeded= his data allowance. Alternative: Simon often =went over= his data allowance. Recede To recede means to go back. Example: Justin ate so many sweets that his gums started to =recede=. Alternative: Justin ate so many sweets that his gums started to =wear back=. Access To access means to enter (go into) something. Something that's accessible can be easily entered or understood. Example: You can =access= the building from three entrances. Alternative: You can =enter= the building through three entrances. Receding Hairline To recede means to go back. Men with receding hairlines start to lose hair from the front of their heads. Think of it like their hairlines are 'going' backwards. Here are some famous examples: Jude Law Prince William Scend - Climb Words containing 'scend' generally relate to climbing. Ascend To ascend is to go up. Example: Paul and Logan were keen to =ascend= the mountain. Alternative: Paul and Logan were keen to =climb= the mountain. Descend To descend is to go down. Example: My grandma =descended= the stairs with difficulty. Alternative: My grandma =went down= the stairs with difficulty. Crescendo A crescendo means a gradual increase, especially in loudness. Example: The song finished with a =crescendo=. Alternative: The song finished by gradually =getting louder=. Descendant A descendant is a relative who comes after you. Think of it like climbing down the family tree - a descendant is a step down. Example: Mary I was a =descendant= of Henry VIII. Alternative: Mary I was a =child= of Henry VIII. Scend - Climb Words containing 'scend' generally relate to climbing. Here are some examples of words containing the root word 'scend': Ascend Descend Crescendo Descendant

resources.title: Colon

content.topicNotes: Using Colons for Lists We already know we need to use commas in lists. But we can also introduce a list with a colon! List of beach items At the beach, we will need: a bucket, spade, rubber dinghy and some armbands. List of pencil case items In my pencil case, there is: a ruler, a sharpener, a pencil, a pen and a rubber. List of clothes In my wardrobe, I have: 2 shirts, 1 pair of jeans, 3 hats and 6 pairs of socks. List of office items In my office, there is: a desk, a lamp, a folder, a filing cabinet and a computer. Shopping Lists Do your parents ever write a shopping list when they go shopping? Next time they do, see if they use a colon to introduce the list. You have already learned that you can introduce lists using a colon. Using Colons to Separate Clauses We don’t always need to use a full stop to separate main clauses. Sometimes, we can use a colon (:). Let's look at some examples... The clock was ticking: midnight was approaching The dog was sad: he lost his bone The boy was hungry: he skipped breakfast Our teacher was angry: the classroom was messy He drove too fast: he crashed his car

resources.title: Colons

content.topicNotes: Using Colons for Lists We already know we need to use commas in lists. But we can also introduce a list with a colon! List of beach items At the beach, we will need**:** a bucket, spade, rubber dinghy and some armbands. List of pencil case items In my pencil case, there is**:** a ruler, a sharpener, a pencil, a pen and a rubber. List of clothes In my wardrobe, I have**:** 2 shirts, 1 pair of jeans, 3 hats and 6 pairs of socks. List of office items In my office, there is**:** a desk, a lamp, a folder, a filing cabinet and a computer.

resources.title: Colour & Shape

content.topicNotes: Photo - Light Words beginning with 'photo' generally relate to light. Photograph A photograph is a picture taken using a camera. The image is made using light. Example: The =photographs= Aaron took in Vietnam were beautiful Alternative: The =pictures= Aaron took in Vietnam were beautiful. Photon A photon is a single unit of light. Example: We learnt about photons in Physics today. Photograph A photograph is a picture taken using a camera. The 'photo' part of the word means 'light' as light enters a camera when a camera takes a picture. Cycl - Circular Words beginning with 'cycl' generally mean something is circular. Cycle A cycle is a series of events that gets repeated. A cycle has circular wheels. Example: Sadie lost her =cycle= so was late to work. Alternative: Sadie lost her =bike= so was late to work. Example: The election =cycle= in the UK repeats every four years. Alternative: The election =pattern= in the UK repeats every four years. Cyclone A cyclone is a type of storm with rotating winds. Example: The =cyclone= destroyed most of the buildings in the city. Alternative: The =storm= destroyed most of the buildings in the city. Cyclical Cyclical events happen one after the other repeatedly. The motion of events is like a circle going round and round repeatedly. Example: Life on Earth is a =cyclical= process. Alternative: Life on Earth happens in =repeated= cycles. Cycl - Circular Words beginning with 'cycl' generally mean something is circular. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'cycl': Cycle Cyclone Cyclical

resources.title: Columns

content.topicNotes: Columns in Writing Columns can be an effective way to help a reader follow a discussion. Columns help because the reader doesn’t have to scan across the page very far. Where can you see columns? Newspapers and magazines use columns. Columns make it easier for readers to read. The writers want reading newspapers and magazines to be quick and easy. Layout Using columns stops readers from thinking your paragraphs are too short. Columns make the writing look longer as the text will go further down the page. The number of columns used can vary depending on what your writing is trying to achieve. Columns in Newspapers Columns make newspapers easier to read

resources.title: Commas

content.topicNotes: Using Commas to Express Meaning You need to use commas to make sure your sentences have the correct meaning. Let's look at an example of how commas can affect meaning... Let's eat Grandpa Without a comma, this sentence means you want to eat Grandpa! Let's eat, Grandpa With a comma, this sentence means you want Grandpa to eat with you. Why don't you sing Roxanne? Without a comma, this question asks someone to sing a song called Roxanne. Why don't you sing, Roxanne? With a comma, this question means you are asking a person called Roxanne to sing. Please call Jasper Without a comma, this sentence means you are asking someone to call Jasper. Please call, Jasper With a comma, this sentence means you are asking Jasper to call you. Commas Change Meanings! Adding a comma to a sentence can change it's meaning completely. Let's look at an example to see how... Please sing Justin This sentence means you're asking someone to sing a song called Justin. Please sing, Justin This sentence means you are asking Justin to sing. Commas Change Meanings! Adding a comma to a sentence can change it's meaning completely. Let's look at an example to see how... Let's eat honey This sentence means you're suggesting people eat honey. Let's eat, honey This sentence means you are asking someone to eat, and calling them the affectionate term 'honey'! Using Commas for Lists You need to use commas in lists to make it clear you are writing a list. Let's look at some examples to see why we use commas... List without commas The children found an acorn a newt conkers and smooth pebbles in the wood. This sentence is very hard to read and very confusing! List with commas The children found an acorn, a newt, conkers and smooth pebbles in the wood. See how much easier the sentence is to read with commas. List without commas The swimmer could do crawl backstroke breaststroke and butterfly beautifully. This sentence is very hard to read and very confusing! List with commas The swimmer could do crawl, backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly beautifully. See how much easier the sentence is to read with commas. List without commas The boy wanted a teddy bear a torch a book a shirt and some shoes for Christmas. This sentence is very hard to read and very confusing! List with commas The boy wanted a teddy bear, a torch, a book, a shirt and some shoes for Christmas. See how much easier the sentence is to read with commas.

resources.title: Commas 2

content.topicNotes: Commas in Compound Sentences We can use commas in compound sentences to break up the different clauses. This makes the sentences easier to read. Let's look at some examples... James is hungry... James is hungry, but he cannot eat until later. Jenny cannot dance... Jenny cannot dance, but she would love to learn. The class has... The class has not yet started, so you should still have time to finish your coffee. The lesson will start late... The lesson will start late, but please still be on time! He is upset... He is upset he lost, yet he still wants to try again. Using Commas for Parenthesis We use parenthesis to add extra information to a sentence. Let's look at how we use commas to add information to sentences... Sammy and Rosie The children, who were called Sammy and Rosie, liked reading. King of the pond The frog, who was king of the pond, wore a crown. Mother's bread The bread, which my mother bakes, is delicious. Past sell-by date The food, which is past its sell-by date, has probably gone off! Soldiers The toy soldiers, that I like to play with, have gone missing.

More examples Please call Jasper. Without a comma, this sentence means you are asking someone to call Jasper. Please call, Jasper. With a comma, this sentence means you are asking Jasper to call you.

content.topicNotes: Using Commas for Lists You need to use commas in lists to make it clear you are writing a list. List without commas The children found an acorn a newt conkers and smooth pebbles in the wood. This sentence is very hard to read and very confusing! List with commas The children found an acorn, a newt, conkers and smooth pebbles in the wood. See how much easier the sentence is to read with commas.
