resources.title: Common Word Roots
Complex Sentences

content.topicNotes: Complex Sentences The other type of sentence you need to know is called a complex sentence. This is how you make a complex sentence... Start with a simple sentence Simple sentence - I heated my food in the microwave. This simple sentence is also called an independent clause. It's called an independent clause because it's a sentence that makes sense by itself. Add a dependent clause A dependent clause is a clause that does NOT make sense by itself. It's called a dependent clause because it depends on another clause to make sense. We will add a dependent clause on the next slide... Dependent clause, then a simple sentence Because it was cold, I heated my food in the microwave. The clause in bold is the dependent clause. The clause does not make sense by itself - we need more information to understand what's going on. This is now a complex sentence. Definition of a complex sentence So a complex sentence is a sentence that contains an independent clause and at least 1 dependent clause. Examples of Complex Sentences A complex sentence is a sentence that contains an independent clause and at least 1 dependent clause. Let's look at some examples... Evil villain When lightning struck, the evil villain Jafar laughed. Shy Pocahontas Although Pocahontas was shy, she spoke to the man. Threatening snake Because the snake was threatening, the boy attacked the snake. Dinosaur bridge The dinosaur could turn into a bridge if the boy needed to cross. Princess Elsa - Complex Sentences A complex sentence is a sentence that contains an independent clause and at least 1 dependent clause. Let's look at some examples using Princess Elsa... Princess Elsa When Princess Elsa touched the stairs, the stairs turned into ice. Icy hands Although Princess Elsa has icy hands, she is never cold. Elsa and Anna If Elsa was playing with Anna, she was happy. Prince Hans Elsa hit Prince Hans because he was in her way. Examples of Complex Sentences You have already learned how to make a complex sentence. Remember - a complex sentence contains an independent clause and at least 1 dependent clause. Let's now look at some more examples of complex sentences... Sentence about being late Although I left the house earlier than normal, I was late for school. The first part of the sentence is the dependent clause. The second part of the sentence is the independent clause. Sentence about a storm After the storm hit, the town was ruined. The first part of the sentence in bold is the dependent clause. The second part of the sentence is the independent clause. Sentence about a ballerina Jemima went to ballet class, even though she could not find her shoes. The first part of the sentence is the independent clause. The second part of the sentence in bold is the dependent clause. Sentence about playing basketball Now that he is so tall, James is good at basketball. The first part of the sentence in bold is the dependent clause. The second part of the sentence is the independent clause. Sentence about rain Since it is raining, I will not go outside. The first part of the sentence in bold is the dependent clause. The second part of the sentence is the independent clause. Examples of Complex Sentences A complex sentence contains an independent clause and at least 1 dependent clause joined by a joining word. Let's now look at some examples of complex sentences... Crying llama When I saw the crying llama, I was very sad. Unhappy King Although the King was very rich, he was very unhappy. Teasing Alice Alice will not stop crying if you keep teasing her. Dumbo's flapping ears Because he sneezed, Dumbo's ears flapped out. Examples of Complex Sentences A complex sentence contains an independent clause and at least 1 dependent clause joined by a joining word. Let's now look at some examples of complex sentences... Jasmine and Aladdin When the carpet flapped, Aladdin and Jasmine kissed. Monster Because the monster scared her, Boo attacked the monster. Angry Maleficent If people disobeyed her, Maleficent became angry. Strong Arthur Although Arthur was young, he was very strong.

resources.title: Compliment & Complement

content.topicNotes: Compliment & Complement Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'compliment' and 'complement'. Compliment I appreciated the compliment. To compliment someone is to say nice things about them. Complement The mango sauce really complemented to ice cream. Complement comes from the word complete. Complementing something means making it complete.

resources.title: Conjunctions
Considering Other Writing

content.topicNotes: Considering Other Stories When you write a story, think about what other authors do. Consider how authors make their characters and settings interesting. Then, you can do the same in your writing. Stories you have read Think about the stories you have read. Think about the techniques the authors used in those stories. Stories you have seen Think about the stories or plays you have seen performed. Think about the techniques the playwrights used to make the play interesting to watch. Stories you have listened to Think about the stories you have listened to. Think about the techniques the author or playwright used to make the story sound interesting.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Coordinating Conjunctions

content.topicNotes: Coordinating Conjunctions Conjunctions are words that connect two sentences or two different parts of sentences together. We use coordinating conjunctions in compound sentences. You can use FANBOYS to remember your co-ordinating conjunctions... __F__or __A__nd __N__or __B__ut __O__r __Y__et __S__o Sentences Using FANBOYS Let's look at some example sentences using the coordinating conjunctions in 'FANBOYS'... __F__or I ate a sandwich, for I was hungry. __A__nd I like horses and I like dogs. __N__or He did not wash up, nor did he flush the toilet! __B__ut I like James but he is mean to me. __O__r You should go to the dentists or you should go to the doctors today. __Y__et The weather was dark and stormy yet we had fun. __S__o I love cooking so I am training to be a chef. Using 'But' as a Conjunction But is a coordinating conjunction. Let's look at some example sentences using the conjunction 'but'... Police chase The policeman chased the robber but he could not catch him. Dancing dog The dog left the party but he could not stop dancing. Big dog The dog was big but he could squeeze through the gate. Using 'Or' as a Conjunction Or is a coordinating conjunction. Let's look at how we can use 'or' in sentences about penguins... Penguin at home The penguin likes to listen to music at home or he likes to sit in silence. Going to the toilet The penguin wees in the toilet or he wees on the floor! Reading penguin The penguin reads comic books or he reads fiction books.

resources.title: Could

content.topicNotes: Could Modal verbs are verbs that affect other verbs in sentences. 'Could' is a modal verb. Could 'Could' means you are able to do something. Examples I could not hear you. You could pay for that. More examples What could I do? How could you face the storm?
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Modal Verbs

resources.title: Creative Fiction Methods

content.topicNotes: Creative Fiction Methods Literary non-fiction uses creative fiction methods that help to engage the reader. Methods Creative fiction methods include: Metaphors & similes Motifs Sensory language Metaphors, similes & motifs Creative fiction methods are used to: Metaphors & similes - help make points in a more abstract way. Motifs - are a repetition of a particular image or idea to make a point. Sensory language Sensory language - means using the senses (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch). Sensory language is used to help the reader imagine the scene or event being described.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Dashes

content.topicNotes: Using Dashes for Parenthesis We use parenthesis to add extra information to a sentence. Let's look at how we use dashes add information to sentences... Fire-breathing dragon A scary dragon - which breathed fire - guarded the castle. Tired dog The dog - which was very tired - slept all day. Year 3 girl The girl - who was in Year 3 - loved painting. Working doctor The doctor - who was on call - missed her dinner. Messy classroom The classroom - which was very messy - needed cleaning. Using Dashes for Parenthesis You have already learned that we can use dashes to add extra information to sentences. Let's look at a few examples... Red car The car - which was red - was fun to drive. Pasta-loving girl The girl - who loved pasta - ate her dinner quickly. Dancing aliens The aliens - who loved to dance - came to the party. Scared dogs The dogs - who were scared - cuddled. Using Dashes to Separate Clauses We don’t always need to use a full stop to separate main clauses. Sometimes we can use a dash (-). Let's look at some examples... The man was curious - he never stopped reading! Johanna is funny - I wish she told me a joke. Patricia likes cats - we will get her one for her birthday. Molly is sad - she had a fight with her best friend. Will adores animals - he is a vegetarian

resources.title: Demands & Commands

content.topicNotes: Using the Subjunctive for Demands and Commands We can use the subjunctive mood to make demands and commands. Demands and commands We can use the subjunctive mood to make demands and commands. The verb of demanding or commanding is always followed by a 'that' clause. Demand The teacher demanded that I tie up my hair. 'Demanded' is the verb of demanding. The 'that' clause follows the verb. Insist Jessica insisted that I give her money. 'Insisted' is the verb of demanding. The 'that' clause follows the verb. Command The officer commanded that the soldier tie his shoelaces. 'Commanded' is the verb of commanding. The 'that' clause follows the verb.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > The Subjunctive Mood

resources.title: Descent & Dissent

content.topicNotes: Descent & Dissent Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'descent' and 'dissent'. Descent The descent was much easier than the ascent. To descend is to go down something. It is the opposite of ascending. Dissent They expressed their dissent by marching outside of parliament. Dissent means refusal or disagreement.

resources.title: Desert & Dessert

content.topicNotes: Desert & Dessert Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'desert' and 'dessert'. Desert There was little water in the desert. A desert is a very dry landscape. Dessert For dessert, there was sticky toffee pudding! Dessert is something sweet eaten after a main meal.

resources.title: Determiners

content.topicNotes: Determiners Determiners help identify which noun you are talking about. What are determiners? Determiners allow you to know: Whether a noun is already known. Whether a noun is being mentioned for the first time. Whether you are singling out a noun. The most common determiners are ‘a’, ‘an’, and ‘the’. The most common determiners The most common determiners are called articles. There are two types of articles: The definite article. The indefinite article. Indefinite or definite article When you haven’t introduced a noun before, you use the indefinite article ‘a’ or ‘an’. E.g. there is a bed in the room. If the noun is already known, you use the definite article ‘the’. E.g. look under the bed in the room. Using articles The definite or indefinite article is used before a noun. E.g. 'the room'. E.g. 'a room'. The definite or indefinite article can also be used before an adjective: E.g. ‘the big room’. E.g. 'a big room'. The Definite & Indefinite Articles Indefinite articles 'A' and 'an' can be used to identify a noun you haven’t introduced before. Definite articles 'The' can be used to identify a noun that's already known. Determiners Determiners help identify which noun you are talking about. Demonstrative determiners Demonstrative determiners tell you where something is. ‘This’ and ‘these’ indicates something is or somethings are close by. ‘That’ and ‘those’ indicates something is or somethings are further away. Possessive determiners Possessive determiners tell you who owns something. ‘My’ and ‘your’, ‘his’ and ‘her’, and ‘its’ and ‘their’ tell you who owns a noun. Demonstrative & Possessive Determiners Demonstrative determiners ‘This’ and ‘these’ indicates something is or somethings are close by. ‘That’ and ‘those’ indicates something is or somethings are further away. Possessive determiners E.g. ‘My’ and ‘your’, ‘his’ and ‘her’, and ‘its’ and ‘their’ tell you who owns a noun.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Word Classes

resources.title: Device & Devise

content.topicNotes: Device & Devise Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'device' and 'devise'. Device He created a device for spreading jam on his toast. A device is a tool or a gadget. Devised She devised a plan for her escape. To devise means to plan or create.

resources.title: Diary Entries

content.topicNotes: Diary Entries A diary is a recount of events in a person’s life, usually written in chronological time order. Content of a diary A diary documents what happens in a person’s life. A diary is written in the first person. A diary is usually structured by providing a date for each diary entry to record when events happened. Diaries explain the writer’s thoughts and feelings about events too. Diaries significance Diaries are usually kept private by the person writing them. Sometimes diaries become widely read and very important to understand history. Diaries have been read and analysed for hundreds of years. Historical importance Reading diaries is a way to explore what life was like in a particular period. Diaries describe life from a person’s perspective (point of view).
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Direct Speech

content.topicNotes: Direct Speech When we use direct speech, we write the exact words someone said. Here are some examples of sentences with direct speech... “Is that him, over there?” shouted Oliver. “Yes, I knew we’d find him!” replied Joe. "Are you enjoying the film?" asked Sally. Examples of Sentences Using Direct Speech When we use direct speech, we write the exact words someone said. Here are some examples... "Do you enjoy being stroked?" "Why is there a chimpanzee in the park?" "I think my kitten is sleepy" "I hope you are hungry!" Using Direct Speech - The Incredibles When we use direct speech, we write the exact words someone said. Let's look at what The Incredibles characters are saying... "You have powers!" said Mr Incredible "I love our family," said Dash "NO CAPES!" said Edna Mode. Using Punctuation for Direct Speech When we are writing direct speech, we need to use the correct punctuation. This is to make sure that the speech looks different from the text surrounding it. Here are some rules you need to know for writing direct speech... Start speech with a capital letter Use speech marks around speech Start a new line for new people speaking End speech with punctuation Speech must end with a punctuation mark (like a full stop or question mark). This punctuation mark has to go inside the speech marks.

resources.title: Disease

content.topicNotes: Osis - Disease Words ending in 'osis' generally refer to states or conditions, particularly diseases or abnormal states. Tuberculosis Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection spread through coughing and sneezing. Example: Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that can be treated. Diagnosis A diagnosis is a judgement or conclusion about what a disease is based on the symptoms. Example: The doctor very quickly =diagnosed= the patient with conjunctivitis. Alternative: The doctor very quickly =determined= that the patient had conjunctivitis. Prognosis A prognosis is an opinion about the likely causes of a disease. A prognosis is also a statement about what's likely to happen in the future - a statement about the 'state' of something in the future. Example: Her =prognosis= was completely incorrect! Alternative: Her =prediction= was completely incorrect! Hypnosis Hypnosis is a mental state that resembles being asleep. People can often be made to do things in this state. Example: While under =hypnosis=, Gregory discussed the car accident. Alternative: While in the =sleeping state=, Gregory discussed the car accident. Hypnosis in the Jungle Book In The Jungle Book, the snake Kaa hypnotises Mowgli. 'Osis' at the end of a word means a state or condition, and hypnosis is a mental state that resembles being asleep. The snake tries to control Mowgli through hyponsis. Kaa hypnotisisng Mowgli being hypnotised Itis - Inflammation Words ending in 'itis' generally mean inflammation or infection of something. Tonsillitis Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils. Bronchitis Bronchitis is an infection of the bronchial tubes. Conjunctivitis Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva in the eye. Hepatitis Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Appendicitis Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix. Meningitis Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges (membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord).

resources.title: Doing & Making

content.topicNotes: Act - Do Words containing the root 'act' generally mean doing something. Action An action is something you do. Example: Bill's dad despaired of Bill's =actions=. Alternative: Bill's dad despaired of =what he was doing=. Interact To interact means to communicate ('do' talking). Example: I want to interact more with my mother.Alternative: I want to speak to my mother more. Activity An activity is a thing you do. Example: What =activities= do you like to do after school? Alternative: What =pastimes= do you like to do after work? React To react means to do something as a response. Example: Ben =reacted= by bursting into tears. Alternative: Ben =responded= by bursting into tears. Act - Do Words containing the root 'act' generally mean doing something. Here are some examples of words containing the root 'act': Action Interact Activity React Fac - Make Words containing 'fac' generally mean doing or making something. Factory A factory is where things are made. Example: Charlie was desperate to visit Willy Wonka's chocolate factory. Facilitate To facilitate means to make something easier to do. Example: Using an iPad in the classroom can =facilitate= learning. Alternative: Using an iPad in the classroom can =improve= learning. Artefact An artefact is something someone has made. Example: The National Taiwan Museum contains many =artefacts= from before the cultural revolution in China. Alternative: The National Taiwan Museum contains many =objects= from before the cultural revolution in China. Willy Wonka's Chocolate Factory A factory is where things are made. Unsurprisingly, Willy Wonka makes chocolate at his chocolate factory in Roald Dahl's book Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. Artefacts at the British Museum Museums house artefacts. Artefacts are things that people have made. The British Museum houses about 8 million artefacts. Here are some of them: Marble lion Kakeimon elephant Terracotta tile from Nimrud, Iraq
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Common Word Roots

resources.title: Draft & Draught

content.topicNotes: Draft & Draught Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'draft' and 'draught'. Draft The first draft of the book took the publishers by surprise. A draft is a rough version of something. Draught A cold draught swept in through the crack in the door. A draught is an air current.

resources.title: Drafting a Layout

content.topicNotes: Choosing the Best Layout You need to make sure you have chosen the best layout for your writing. Let's look at some examples. Newspaper If you are writing a newspaper piece, you will need to use: columns a headline Non-fiction (information writing) If you are writing a non-fiction piece of writing, you might need to use: sub-headings a caption Formal letter If you are writing a formal letter, you will need to have at the top: your address the date the address of the person you are writing
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Drafting a Narrative

content.topicNotes: Drafting a Narrative (Story) When you are writing a narrative, you need to think about a few things. Describing the setting well You need to describe the setting in detail. This helps to build an image in your reader's head. Some interesting settings might be: a haunted house, a beautiful beach, a battlefield, etc. Creating interesting characters You need to create interesting characters. Creating an exciting atmosphere You need to create an exciting atmosphere. This helps to make your story interesting. Using dialogue You need to use dialogue. A dialogue is a conversation between characters. Dialogues help your reader get to know your characters better.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Drafting: Grammar

content.topicNotes: Drafting: Grammar What is drafting? Drafting means doing a rough piece of work that you plan to make better later on. You need to think about your grammar when you are drafting. Use grammar correctly Make sure you are using your grammar correctly. Layout Make sure that how your writing looks is easy for the reader to understand. Layout means how your writing looks on the page. Vocabulary Make sure you are using lots of different vocabulary. Using different vocabulary makes your writing exciting. Why write a draft? Writing a draft allows you to: Write down and organise all of your thoughts. Improve your writing at a later stage more easily.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Drafting: Precising

content.topicNotes: Cutting Down Your Writing 'Précising' is a fancy word for 'cutting down'. You should try to cut down any long passages. Cutting down You should try to avoid long passages. Shorter passages are easier to read. Shorter passages can still contain all the important details. Example: original passage Henry is a boy. Henry is a boy at my school. Henry does not have many friends. Henry sits by himself at lunchtime. Henry sits by himself at break time. Henry sits by himself in the classroom. I want to talk to Henry. I do not know how to talk to Henry. We could cut this passage down without losing any meaning. Example: new passage Henry is a boy at my school. Henry does not have many friends. Henry sits by himself at lunchtime, at break time and in the classroom. I want to talk to Henry but I do not know how. We have cut out some of the repetition. We have used different sentences to make the passage shorter. Cutting Down Your Writing: Another Example Original passage I do not like Jacob. Do you want to know why I do not like Jacob? I am going to list all the reasons why I do not like Jacob. Rhetorical question The passage above have a rhetorical question. A rhetorical question is a question that does not expect an answer. The rhetorical question in the passage above is for effect. So we might not want to lose the rhetorical question. But we can still cut down the passage. New passage I do not like Jacob. Do you want to know why? I am going to list the reasons why. By cutting out the repetition, we have shortened the passage.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Editing: Editing Your Tenses

content.topicNotes: Editing Your Tenses Your tense needs to be the same and correct throughout a piece of writing. Tenses You need to use the same tenses throughout a piece of writing. This doesn’t always mean the tense needs to be the same the entire narrative For example, a flashback may be in a different tense. But, the tense needs to be the same within a section of writing. Correct example I caught the bus. I went to school. I ate my lunch. I talked to my friends. These sentences all use the past tense. Incorrect example My name is Jenny. I was eight years old. I like going swimming and cycling. Not all the verbs in this sentence are in the right tense. Most of the verbs are in the present tense. The odd one out is 'was', which is in the past tense. The sentence should be: I am eight years old. Good example I have a dog. He is often sleepy. He sleeps with my brother. He sleeps on walks. But he does not sleep on his skateboard! These sentences all use the present tense. Bad example Lily loved her teddy bear. When he goes missing, she was very sad. Not all the verbs in this sentence are in the right tense. Most of the verbs are in the past tense. The odd one out is 'goes', which is in the past tense. The correct sentence should be: When he went missing, she was very sad.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Editing: Things to Check When Editing

content.topicNotes: Things to Check When Editing When you are editing your writing, you will need to check different things. The effectiveness of your writing You will need to check how effective your writing is. Think about its purpose, and the reader it is aimed at. Formality You will need to check that you are using the correct formality. informal or formal This will depend on both text type and reader. For example: A letter to your teacher will be very formal. A story you write for your friends will not be very formal. Other things to check grammar, vocabulary, punctuation spelling plurals and singulars
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Editing: What Is Editing?

content.topicNotes: What is Editing? You will have planned and drafted your writing. It is now time to edit! So what is editing? Editing Editing is when we read over our work and check for any errors or changes we can make. Original sentences (1) James is my freind. We always get the bus together And eat our lunch together. If you edit these sentences, you will notice a few mistakes: There is a spelling mistake. There is a capital letter used incorrectly. Edited sentences (1) James is my friend. We always get the bus together and eat our lunch together. Original sentences (2) john is a funny boy. john makes me laugh not he tells jokes. If you edit these sentences, you will notice that: John's name is missing a capital letter. The word 'not' does not make sense. You could use different words instead of 'not'. Edited sentences (2) John is a funny boy. John makes me laugh when he tells jokes.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Ellipses

content.topicNotes: Ellipses An ellipsis (…) is used to imply that a word, a sentence or a whole section from a text has been deliberately left out. Ellipses can also be used to create pauses in a sentence. Remove unnecessary information An ellipsis can be used to show that the beginning of a sentence has been left out. E.g. ‘…we arrived after the movie began.’ The use of an ellipsis at the beginning of a sentence shows something happens before what you read. The beginning of the sentence was removed because the words after the ellipsis contain the most important information. To suggest there is more to know An ellipsis can be used to suggest that there is more to an idea than the writer is telling you. An ellipsis is normally used to suggest there is more to an idea at the end of a paragraph or story. E.g. ‘Suddenly John turned, and what he saw changed him forever…’ To cut down a quote Some quotes can be quite long. You can begin a quote and then use an ellipsis to remove the less important parts of the quote. E.g. 'Darwin wrote about his Theory of Evolution...in 1859.' To cut down a quote example ‘The instruments of darkness…to betray us in deepest consequence.’ The beginning of the quote is important. The end of the quote is important. The middle of the quote is NOT as important.The ellipsis shows there is more to the quote, but the information is NOT important. To express hesitation An ellipsis can be used to show hesitation. E.g. ‘I don’t know…where they are.’ E.g. ‘I….don't…want…to.’ Uses of Ellipses An ellipsis can be used to: Express hesitation 'I...can't...reach' Cut down a quote Suggest there is more to know Remove unnecessary information

resources.title: Empty & Broken

content.topicNotes: Vac - Empty Words beginning with 'vac' generally mean being empty. Vacate To vacate means to leave somewhere so that it becomes empty (of people). Example: When the fire alarm went off, the workers =vacated= the building immediately. Alternative: When the fire alarm went off, the workers =cleared out= of the building immediately. Vacuum A vacuum is a space with no matter in it. A vacuum also means a lack of something. Example: Outer space is a =vacuum=. Alternative: There is =no matter= in outer space. Vacuous Vacuous means empty. When used to talk about people, vacuous can mean unintelligent ('empty' headed). Example: My grandma had a =vacuous= expression on her face when I opened the door. Alternative: My grandma had an =empty= expression on her face when I opened the door. The Vacuum Cleaner A vacuum cleaner works by creating a vacuum, which is a space with no matter in, to suck up dirt from the floor. The 'vac' part of vacuum means empty, as a vacuum is empty space. Frac - Breaking Words beginning with 'frac' or 'frag' generally refer to breaking. Fracture To fracture is to crack or break. A fracture is a crack or break in a hard object. Example: Kenji =fractured= his clavicle playing rugby. Alternative: Kenji =broke= his collarbone playing rugby. Fraction A fraction is a small portion of the whole. Think of a fraction like a broken off bit of a broken whole! In maths, a fraction is a broken up whole number. Example: She closed her eyes for a =fraction= of a second but still missed seeing the bird. Alternative: She closed her eyes for a =split= second but still missed seeing the bird. Example: $$\frac{1}{2}$$ is a fraction. Fragment To fragment is to break something up into pieces. A fragment is a broken off piece of something. Example: The shop floor was covered in =fragments= of glass. Alternative: The shop floor was covered in =pieces= of glass. Dur - Hard Words beginning with 'dur' generally refer to something being hard or lasting. Duration Duration is the length of time something lasts. Example: I slept for the =duration= of the maths class. Alternative: I slept for the =length= of the maths class. During During either means from the start to finish of a specific time period (while a time period 'lasts') or at some point during a specific time period. Example: =During= Ramadan, most Muslims fast. Alternative: =Throughout= Ramadan, most Muslims fast. Example: The police officer was shot =during= the raid. Alternative: The police officer was shot =at some point in= the raid. Durable Something that's durable can last a long time. Example: I'm glad I bought these boots - they're made of such =durable= leather! Alternative: I'm glad I bought these boots - they're made of such =long-lasting= leather! Duress Duress are threats ('hard' actions) or other violent actions used to get people to do things against their will. Example: The robber committed the crime under =duress=. Alternative: The robber committed the crime under =pressure=.

resources.title: Fact & Opinion

content.topicNotes: Fact & Opinion It is important to be able to recognise the difference between fact and opinion when we are reading. Opinions An opinion is what someone thinks. Different people may have the same or different opinions. There is no right or wrong. Opinion: example Giraffes are the most interesting animals. Facts A fact is a true statement. Facts are things that have happened or that can be proven using evidence. Fact: example World Giraffe Day is on the 21st of June.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Fact & Opinion - Questions

content.topicNotes: Fact vs. Opinion You can be asked questions that ask you for facts. You could also be asked to recognise other people's opinions. Fact or opinion questions Fact or opinion questions are often set out as tables. The tables often have a set of statements. Each statement will have an option to tick 'fact' or 'opinion' beside it. Spotting opinions in a text To check if a statement is an opinion, we can ask: Does the statement describe a feeling or belief? Might someone else hold a different point of view? The statement is an opinion if the answer is yes to either of those questions. Spotting facts in a text To check if a statement is a fact, we can ask: Is the statement telling us something that can be proven with evidence from the text? Would two people with the same evidence give the same answer? The statement is a fact if the answer is yes to either of those questions.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Fair & Fare

content.topicNotes: Fair and Fare Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Fair That is not fair! Fair means treating people equally or in the right way. Fare You need to pay your bus fare. A fare is an amount of money you pay for travelling in a vehicle. Types of Fares A fare is an amount of money you pay for travelling in a vehicle. Do not confuse the word fare with the word fair, which means treating people equally. Let's look at some different types of fares... Bus fare Taxi fare

resources.title: Famous Diaries

content.topicNotes: Famous Diaries Famous diaries include Samuel Pepys’ diary and Anne Frank’s ‘Diary of a Young Girl’ Samuel Pepys’ diary Samuel Pepys’ diary was written between 1660 and 1669. Samuel Pepys’ diary described events such as the Great Fire of London. Samuel Pepys’ diary is still studied today. Anne's ‘Diary of a Young Girl’ Anne Frank’s ‘Diary of a Young Girl’ is a well-known diary. Anne's diary details the Jewish Frank family hiding in a secret annexe during World War Two to escape capture by German forces. Anne's diary describes their time in the annexe, including their daily life, worries, and even normal family arguments. Anne's diary ending Tragically, the final diary entry is dated 1st August 1944. Anne and her family were captured three days later and sent to a concentration camp. Only Anne's father survived, and he later went on to publish Anne’s diary as a way of remembering victims of the Holocaust.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Famous Letters

content.topicNotes: Famous Letters Martin Luther King’s ‘Letter from Birmingham Jail’ is an example of a famous historical letter. Letter from Birmingham Jail ‘Letter from Birmingham Jail’ was written in response to a newspaper article. That newspaper article criticised Martin Luther King after he was arrested for protesting against segregation in 1963. Abolishing segregation ‘Letter from Birmingham Jail’ is eleven pages long. In the letter Martin Luther King passionately argues to abolish segregation in the United States. Segregation in the U.S. was the enforced racial separation in public spaces and services. ‘I have a dream’ speech Martin Luther King’s similarly famous ‘I have a dream’ speech took place four months after he wrote this letter.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Farther & Father

content.topicNotes: Farther & Father Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'farther' and 'father'. Farther As they got farther into the maze, they lost track of where they were. Farther means the same as further. Father His father was a fisherman. A father is a parent who is male (dad).

resources.title: Features of a Script

content.topicNotes: Features of a Script Scripts are written for drama performances including plays, television shows, films, and radio shows. Purpose Scripts are used by directors and actors or performers. Scripts have a particular layout that is easy to follow so they can focus on their performance. Acts and scenes Play scripts are organised in: Acts Scenes - smaller parts of acts A new scene will begin if the location of the action or time period changes. Stage directions at the start of each scene will make it clear where it takes place and when. Characters and stage directions The script will describe the characters of the play, their clothing or appearance, and any props (objects) needed on stage. Stage directions may describe how a character moves on stage or their facial expressions. Stage directions are in italics to make them stand out from the rest of the script. Dialogue The character's speech is called a dialogue. The character’s speech will start with their name in capital letters on the left. Each new speaker starts on a new line. Stage directions are also sometimes used at the start of the dialogue. Stage directions are put in brackets to describe how the character says a line, such as ‘excitedly’ or ‘giggling’.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing formats

resources.title: Features of a Speech

content.topicNotes: Features of a Speech Speeches are a powerful way to communicate ideas or opinions. Speeches should be structured carefully to engage the listener and make the perspective on a particular topic clear. An opening Speeches need an attention-grabbing opening in order to engage the listeners. An opening can use a range of different forms: A rhetorical question, An interesting fact or statistic Powerful imagery The structure Use a clear but simple structure so that your listener can follow your argument. Decide on the most important points in your speech and put these first. Make sure you have one viewpoint that is explained throughout the speech. Make sure your perspective and opinion are clear. Non-fiction methods A range of non-fiction methods should be included in a speech. Non-fiction methods include facts and statistics to provide information. Persuasive methods like rhetorical questions, direct address and repetition should also be included. Like in an article, anecdotes can be used in order to help give examples on a particular topic or present certain experiences. A conclusion End with an impactful conclusion. A conclusion may be a point that is important and easy for your audience to remember. A conclusion can also be an action that you would like your listener to take after the speech.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing formats

resources.title: Figurative & Emotive Language

content.topicNotes: Figurative & Emotive Language Emotive language Emotive language is when language is used to create a strong emotional response – this could be any emotion, such as anger, excitement, happiness, sadness, etc. E.g. The sad, downcast dog drooped its little head. Figurative language Figurative language is using figures of speech to be more effective, persuasive or impactful. Such devices include metaphors and similes. E.g. My bedroom is a freezer! Figurative Language Figurative language is using figures of speech to be more effective, persuasive or impactful. Such devices include metaphors and similes. Here are some examples: The wind is a howling wolf (metaphor) The birthday boy is like an excitable puppy (simile) The storm scooped the poor lady up (personification)

resources.title: For & Against

content.topicNotes: Pro - For Words beginning in 'pro' can mean being for something or in a forward direction. The prefix 'pro' has lots of other meanings, like being 'in front of' something, but here we will only look at the forward meaning. Propel To propel means to push or drive forward. Example: The wind helped to =propel= the boat forward. Alternative: The wind helped to =drive= the boat forward. Pro To be pro something means to be in favour of it. A pro is also an advantage of something. Example: Sebastian was =pro= the idea of his school abolishing homework. Alternative: Sebastian was =for= the idea of his school abolishing homework. Example: A =pro= of living on the outskirts of a city is that it is often cheaper. Alternative: An =advantage= of living on the outskirts of a city is that it is often cheaper. Proceed To proceed means to go forwards. Example: We will =proceed= with this matter no further. Alternative: We will =go forward= with this matter no further. Proclaim To proclaim is to announce something publicly - to put 'forward' your thoughts publicly. Example: The government =proclaimed= that the war was over. Alternative: The government =announced= that the war was over. Propellers Propellers are mechanical devices that help ships and aircraft to move. The prefix 'pro' means forward, so think of propellers as devices driving things 'forward'. Here are some things that use propellers: Drones (aircraft) Planes Happy football players Helicopters Anti - Against Words beginning with 'anti' generally mean being against or opposed to something. Antibiotic An antibiotic is a substance used to destroy microorganisms and treat infections. Example: My brother is taking antibiotics because he has tonsillitis. Antisocial Antisocial means not social or against society. Example: Henry will not go to the party because he is too =antisocial=. Alternative: Henry will not go to the party because he =doesn't like socialising=. Example: Stealing is an example of =antisocial= behaviour. Alternative: Stealing is an example of =wrong= behaviour. Anticlimax A climax is a build up towards something really exciting. So an anticlimax is when something is not as exciting or impressive as expected, so it causes disappointment. Example: The book's ending was an =anticlimax=. Alternative: The book's ending was a =disappointment=. Antibacterial Something that's antibacterial is designed to kill bacteria - it's 'against' bacteria. Example: I shouldn't have touched that dirty plate - I don't have any =antibacterial= gel with me. Alternative: I shouldn't have touched that dirty plate - I don't have any =bacteria-killing= gel with me. Anti - Against Words beginning with 'anti' generally mean being against or opposed to something. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'anti': Antibiotic Antisocial Anticlimax Antibacterial Contra - Against Words beginning with 'contra' generally mean against something. Contrast A contrast is a difference between two or more things. Example: Molly and Georgia have =contrasting= hair colours. Alternative: Molly and Georgia have =opposite= hair colours. Contradict To contradict means to say that something is wrong, or to say the opposite of what someone has said. Example: The dictator said the captives deserved to be punished, and no one =contradicted= him. Alternative: The dictator said the captives deserved to be punished, and no one =said he was wrong=. Example: Jessica said the journey was pleasant; Hattie =contradicted= her by saying the journey was awful. Alternative: Jessica said the journey was pleasant; Hattie =opposed= her by saying the journey was awful Contrary Contrary means opposite in nature - 'against' the nature of something. On the contrary is a common phrase meaning opposite to. Example: Patrick thought the fleece was ugly. I, =on the contrary=, thought the fleece was beautiful. Alternative: Patrick thought the fleece was ugly. I, =on the other hand=, thought the fleece was beautiful. Example: The results of the match were =contrary= to my expectations. Alternative: The results of the match were the =opposite= of what I expected. Contraception Contraception is the use of different methods to prevent pregnancy. More literally, contraception means 'against' conception, which is the act of conceiving a child. Example: Condoms are a cheap and effective means of =contraception=. Alternative: Condoms are a cheap and effective means of =birth control=.

resources.title: Full Stops

content.topicNotes: Full Stops Full stops place a strong boundary around an idea. Full stops are important because they signal that one idea is over. Where to use full stops Full stops can be used at the end of sentences that are: Statements. Commands. A sentence needs to have a main clause that makes sense on its own. A sentence does NOT need further information to complete its meaning. Separating main clauses You should use a full stop when separating two main clauses. E.g. Seneca is fun. I like cookies. Joining main clauses Sometimes we want to join two main clauses together. You can join two main clauses together using a coordinating conjunction (e.g. and, but, so, for). E.g. Seneca is fun and I like cookies. You would usually place a comma before the conjunction if the clauses are reasonably long. Examples of Sentences You can join two main clauses together using a coordinating conjunction. Some examples of coordinating conjunctions are: And I sat at the table and ate my dinner. But I would like to eat more but I am full. So I won't eat any more so I'll save it for later. For I can't move now for I ate too much.

resources.title: Grate & Great

content.topicNotes: Grate and Great Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Grate You should grate the cheese for the sandwich. To grate means to shred. Great You are great! Great means really good! Grate and Great Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Grate (to shred) Great (really good) Grated Foods To grate means to shred. We can grate different foods to enjoy them in different ways. Do not confuse the word 'grate' with the word 'great', which means really good. Let's look at some examples of grated foods... Grated cheese Grated carrot Grated beetroot

resources.title: Great & Greater

content.topicNotes: Magn - Great Words beginning with 'magn' generally mean something is great or large. Magnificent Something that is magnificent is very great, beautiful or impressive. Example: Westminster Abbey is a =magnificent= building. Alternative: Westminster Abbey is a =very impressive= building. Magnitude The magnitude of something is the great size of it. Example: Percy was intimidated by the =magnitude= of the task. Alternative: Percy was intimidated by the =great size= of the task. Magnanimous Magnanimous means very forgiving or generous. The word is often when a superior is showing forgiveness or generosity towards an inferior. Example: The leader was =magnanimous= in victory and commended the losing team. Alternative: The leader was =kind= in victory and commended the losing team. Magnate A magnate is someone who is very successful, wealthy and influential. Example: Many people consider my father to be an influential technology =magnate=. Alternative: Many people consider my father to be an influential technology =businessman=. Maj - Greater Words beginning with 'maj' generally mean greater than something. Major Major means more important, impressive or significant than other things. Example: Smoking is a =major= cause of lung cancer. Alternative: Smoking is one of the =greatest= causes of lung cancer. Majesty Something with majesty demands a lot of respect. It does this because it's better or greater than other things. The title His or Her Majesty is used for kings and queens - who are superior to the rest of the population. Example: The song 'I will always love you' by Whitney Houston has =majesty=. Alternative: The song 'I will always love you' by Whitney Houston has =power=. Majority The majority is the greater number. Example: The =majority= of people think that murder is wrong. Alternative: =Most= people think that murder is wrong. Major in the Army Major is a rank in the British Army. The prefix 'maj' means greater than, and a major is 'greater' in rank than a captain. Mult - Many Words beginning with 'mult' generally mean much or many of something. Multiply To multiply something means to increase it by a certain amount. So you make something many times bigger than it was before. Example: Bacteria can =multiply= rapidly in the right conditions. Alternative: Bacteria can =increase in number= rapidly in the right conditions. Multitude A multitude is a great number of things. Example: Jenny decorated her house with a =multitude= of paintings. Alternative: Jenny decorated her house with a =vast number= of paintings. Multiple Multiple means having many different parts. Example: Peter went to the gym =multiple= times a week. Alternative: Peter went to the gym =many= times a week. Multinational Multinational means involving many nations. Example: Nike is a successful =multinational= company. Alternative: Nike is a successful company, =operating in many countries=. Multipurpose Multipurpose meaning having many functions. Example: My dad swore by his =multipurpose= tool. Alternative: My dad swore by his =multifunctional= tool. Multimedia Multimedia means involving many different types of media (e.g. still picture, video). Example: The =multimedia= presentation allowed the audience to read, watch and listen. Alternative: The presentation, =which used many different media forms=, allowed the audience to read, watch and listen. Mult - Many Words beginning with 'mult' generally mean much or many of something. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'mult': Multiply Multitude Multinational Multimedia

resources.title: Groan & Grown

content.topicNotes: Groan and Grown Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Groan I had to get out of bed, which made me groan. A groan is the noise you make when you're annoyed or upset. Try and do one now! Grown When I saw him again, he had grown! Grown means got taller or bigger.

resources.title: Guessed & Guest

content.topicNotes: Guessed & Guest Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'guessed' and 'guest'. Guessed You guessed the answer correctly! Guessed is the past tense of guess. Guest She was the first guest they had had in years. A guest is a visitor, usually to someone’s home.

resources.title: Hard & Soft 'c' Sounds

content.topicNotes: Hard ‘c’ Sounds Words that are spelt with a ‘c’ are pronounced with either a 'k' sound (which sounds hard) or an 's' sound (which sounds soft). ‘__k__’ sound If the word that is spelt with a ’c’ has an ‘a’, ‘u’ or ‘o’ straight after the 'c', the 'c' makes a 'k' sound. 'Cat' is pronounced with a 'k' sound. 'Catch' is pronounced with a 'k' sound. 'Curtain' is pronounced with a 'k' sound. 'Cucumber' is pronunced with a 'k' sound. 'Community' is pronunced with a 'k' sound. 'Computer' is pronunced with a 'k' sound. 'cc' For a 'cc' in a word to form a 'k' sound, all of the following must be true: The word has more than 1 syllable. The 'cc' sound is in-between 2 vowels. The 1st vowel is a short sound.E.g. occupy, succulent, tobacco. 'k' The 'k' sound is spelt with a 'k' if: The 'k' sound follows a consonant or a long vowel. Or the 'k' sound follows a long vowel sound.E.g. milk, make, tank, soak, bark. Spellings with a 'k' Sound Soccer A 'cc' forms a 'k' sound if all of the following is true: The word has more than 1 syllable. The 'cc' sound is in-between 2 vowels. The 1st vowel is a short sound. Chalk The 'k' sound is spelt with a 'k' if: The 'k' sound follows a consonant or a long vowel. Or the 'k' sound follows a long vowel sound. Cut If the word that is spelt with a ’c’ has an ‘a’, ‘u’ or ‘o’ straight after the 'c', the 'c' makes a 'k' sound. The Hard ‘c’ Sound from a 'ck' Words that are spelt with a ‘c’ are pronounced with either a 'k' sound (which sounds hard) or an 's' sound (which sounds soft). 'ck' If a word has one syllable and the 'k' sound comes after a short vowel sound, then the 'k' sound is spelt ‘__ck__’. 'Sack' is one syllable and the 'c' comes after a short vowel sound so 'ck' is used. 'Back' is one syllable and the 'c' comes after a short vowel sound so 'ck' is used. 'Clock' is one syllable and the 'c' comes after a short vowel sound so 'ck' is used. 'ck' 'ck' is used instead of 'cc' if the letter after the 'k' sound is a ‘y’, ‘e’, or ‘i’. E.g. lucky, blackest, picking, ticking. Spellings with a 'k' Sound Jockey 'ck' is used instead of 'cc' if the letter after the 'k' sound is a ‘y’, ‘e’, or ‘i’. Lock If a word has one syllable and the 'k' sound comes after a short vowel sound, then the 'k' sound is spelt ‘__ck__’. Soft 'c' Sounds Words that are spelt with a ‘c’ are pronounced with either a 'k' sound (which sounds hard) or an 's' sound (which sounds soft). 'c' followed by an 'e' You pronounce 'c' with an 's' sound if the ‘c’ has an ‘e’ straight after. For example: Celery. Ceiling. Receive. Receipt. Censored. 'c' followed by an 'i' You pronounce 'c' with an 's' sound if the ‘c’ has an ‘i’ straight after. For example: Pencil. Circle. Precise. 'c' followed by a 'y' You pronounce 'c' with an 's' sound if the ‘c’ has an ‘y’ straight after. For example: Cycle. Cyclops. Words with a Soft 'c' Sound Censored The 'c' is followed by an 'e'. The 'c' makes an 's' sound. Pencil The 'c' is followed by an 'i'. The 'c' makes an 's' sound. Recycle The 'c' is followed by a 'y'. The first 'c' makes an 's' sound. The second 'c' makes a 'k' sound. Celery The 'c' is followed by an 'e'. The 'c' makes an 's' sound.

content.topicNotes: Spelling Rules for the Hard 'U' Sound The hard 'u' sound is spelt 'ou' in many words. Let's look at some common words spelt with 'ou'... Young Touch Double Trouble Tough Rough Spelling Rules for the Hard 'U' Sound The hard 'u' sound is spelt 'ou' in many words. Let's look at some common words spelt with 'ou'... Let's look at some words that are spelt with a 'y'... Myth A myth is a traditional story. It can also be a story that lots of people think is true, but is actually false! Gym A gym is a place people go to exercise. Mystery A mystery is something that's isn't understood yet and still needs explaining. For example, detectives solve mysteries. resources.title: Have to

content.topicNotes: Have to Model verbs are verbs that affect other verbs in sentences. 'Have to' and 'has to' are modal verbs. Have to 'Have to' and 'has to' are used to show that something needs to happen. Examples I have to meet my boss. We have to go riding again soon. More examples You have to visit Spain. You have to make an appointment.

resources.title: Headings & Subheadings

content.topicNotes: Headings Headings are used to help structure and organise your writing in some non-fiction texts. Non-fiction texts include reports, reviews, articles, informative texts and speeches. What is a heading? A heading is like a title but not quite the same. A title summarises the entire piece of writing. A heading summarises a particular point or points that are closely connected. A heading acts as a marker of a new point of discussion. Creating headings When planning your writing, you should write out the main points that you know will help your argument. The points you write out will become your headings. You can also write headings by summarising the main points into a word or two (5 words at the most). Where to put headings A heading is usually on its own line in a text. A heading is on its own line so it clearly stands out. The power of headings Headings signpost your discussion by helping the reader get an instant overview of what your next point will be. Headings also allow the reader to navigate around your writing. The reader can skip some sections if necessary to get to the point that is most relevant to them. Headings also break up longer texts making them easier to process. Subheadings Subheadings help organise non-fiction writing by signposting new points. Using subheadings Sometimes a major idea will be complex and involve multiple points. Each point can be closely related. But each point may benefit from being discussed separately. Subheadings could be used to separate the closely related points. Creating subheadings Once you have identified your main points, each separate idea in the main points can be separated using subheadings. Each subheading should summarise what is in that section (using up to 5 words if necessary). Each subheading should be on its own line in your text so it clearly stands out.

resources.title: Heal, Heel & He'll

content.topicNotes: Heal, Heel and He'll Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Heel The heel of my foot hurts after dancing. Your heel is the round part at the back of your foot. Heal The doctor can heal you. To heal is to cure someone. He'll He'll be out later. He'll is the short form of 'he will'. Mr Bean the Doctor! Mr Bean is pretending to be a doctor here. A doctor's job is to heal people. Do not confuse the word heal with the words 'heel' (which means the round part of your foot) or 'he'll' (which is the shortened version of 'he will'). These 3 words are homophones! Jesus the Healer In the Bible, it says that Jesus was a healer. Do not confuse the word heal with the words 'heel' (which means the round part of your foot) or 'he'll' (which is the shortened version of 'he will'). These 3 words are homophones!

resources.title: Hear & Here

content.topicNotes: Here and Hear Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Here Come here! Here is the place you are. Hear Do you hear the band? To hear means your ears pick up noise. Dumbo Dumbo has very big ears. So Dumbo can probably hear very well. Do not confuse the word 'hear' with the word 'here', which is the place you are. 'Here' and 'hear' sound the same because they are homophones.

resources.title: Heard & Herd

content.topicNotes: Heard & Herd Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'heard' and 'herd'. Heard I heard great things about the show. Heard is the past tense of hear. Herd A herd of sheep move from one field to the next. A herd is how we describe groups of certain animals.

resources.title: Hearing & Speaking

content.topicNotes: Aud - Hear Words beginning with 'aud' generally relate to hearing. Audible Something that's audible can be heard. Example: The radio was playing so quietly it was barely =audible=. Alternative: The radio was playing so quietly it was barely =hearable=. Audience An audience listens to a performance. Example: Even though the =audience= didn't enjoy they play, they still clapped at the end. Alternative: Even though the =spectators= didn't enjoy the play, they still clapped at the end. Audio Audio means sound. Example: =Audio= devices are becoming more common. Alternative: =Sound= devices are becoming more common. Aud - Hear Words beginning with 'aud' generally relate to hearing. Here are some examples of words that begin with the prefix 'aud': Audible Audience Audio Dict - Say Words beginning with 'dict' generally mean something about speaking. Dictionary A dictionary lists all the words of a language and their meanings. Example: I learnt what the word 'onomatopoeia' means by looking it up in the dictionary. Dictate To dictate means to give orders or to say something aloud. Example: The general =dictated= the terms for peace. Alternative: The general =ordered= the terms for peace. Example: Caitlin =dictated= to her secretary the email she wanted to send. Alternative: Caitlin =said aloud= to her secretary the email she wanted to send. Dictaphone A dictaphone is a device that records people speaking. Example: Journalists often use dictaphones in interviews so that they don't have to write everything someone says down. Dictator A dictator is a ruler with total power - dictators have say over everything. Example: Stalin was a dictator who ruled Russia from 1929 to 1953. Alternative: Stalin was an =autocrat= who ruled Russia from 1929 to 1953. Dictators Words beginning with 'dict' generally mean something about speaking. A dictator is a ruler with total power - dictators have 'say' over everything. Here are some examples of famous dictators: Joseph Stalin (USSR) Adolf Hitler (Nazi Germany) Benito Mussolini (Italy) Kim Jong-un (North Korea)

Hopes & Wishes

content.topicNotes: Using the Subjunctive for Hopes and Wishes We use the subjunctive mood to talk about imagined situations. Hopes and wishes We use the subjunctive mood to talk about imagined situations. So we can use the subjunctive to show hopes and wishes. Use 'if' and 'were' To create an imagined situation, we need to make a clause using 'if' and 'were'. If I were rich... If I were a princess... Add 'would', 'could', or 'might' Now, we need to show what would happen in these imagined situations. We do this by adding a clause containing 'would', 'could' or 'might'. If it were to snow, I might get the day off school! Examples If I were a princess, I would ride a dragon. If I were rich, I could buy a sports car.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > The Subjunctive Mood

resources.title: Hopes & Wishes: Examples

content.topicNotes: Using the Subjunctive for Hopes and Wishes: Examples You have already learned that you can use the subjunctive to show hopes and wishes. Now, let's look at some examples... If I were to become a prince... If I were to become a prince, I would buy 100 horses. If it were to rain... If it were to rain tomorrow, I might get a lift from my sister. If Ben were to find... If Ben were to find my phone charger, I could call my friend. If you were to become a doctor... If you were to become a doctor, you could cure lots of illnesses.

resources.title: Hyphens

content.topicNotes: Using Hyphens Hyphens are dashes that we use between words that describe a noun. So words with hyphens are adjectives. Hyphens Hyphens are dashes. We use hyphens between words that describe a noun. So words with hyphens are adjectives. This is a hyphen: - The boy had sky blue eyes When there is no dash, it is not clear what this sentence means. 'Sky' is a noun. 'Blue' is an adjective. The boy had sky=-=blue eyes When there is a dash, we know that the eyes are sky-blue coloured. 'Sky-blue' is an adjective. The girl was cold hearted When there is no dash, is it not clear what this sentence means. The two adjectives 'cold' and 'hearted' seem unrelated. The girl was cold=-=hearted When there is a dash, it is clear that the girl is not very affectionate. The adjective 'cold-hearted' means that she is not affectionate.

resources.title: Hyphens

content.topicNotes: Hyphens Hyphens are used to join words together. Hyphens tell us that 2 or more words in a sentence are linked. There are quite a few different uses of hyphens: Compound adjectives Compound adjectives are linked adjectives that are used before a noun. For example: ‘A multi-storey building’. ‘A state-of-the-art design’. The adjectives are linked to create an overall adjective. Avoiding confusion Sometimes a hyphen helps avoid confusion when words can have more than one meaning. E.g. ‘John recovered the cushions’ means something different to ‘John re-covered the cushions’. Writing on a new line Hyphens can be used to break up a word if it continues onto the next line. A hyphen can only break up a word between two syllables in a word. For example:It was only that night that I dis-covered where they were hiding. Prefixes Hyphens are used in words that begin with the prefixes 'self', 'ex' and 'all'. E.g. self-assured, self-doubt. E.g. ex-con, ex-professional. E.g. all-knowing, all-expenses paid. Hyphens in Names and Numbers Hyphens are used to join words together. Hyphens tell us that 2 or more words in a sentence are linked. Here are some more examples of how you can use hyphens. Double-barrelled last names People with double-barrelled last names use a hyphen to separate their two last names. For example: William Jones-Smith. Sandra McCartney-Philips. Hyphens to write numbers We use hyphens when writing numbers as words: Fractions (e.g. it was one-quarter of the amount). Compound numbers after 21 (e.g. My Dad is forty-two years old). Hyphens for a range We also use hyphens to give a range: Times (e.g. 9:15-10:15). Between numbers of people (e.g. 320-450 Americans). Between page numbers (e.g. p 200-250). Between dates (e.g. 1990-2000).

resources.title: Identifying Your Audience

content.topicNotes: Identifying your Audience Think about your audience when planning your writing. Who are you writing to? You need to think about who will read your writing when you plan it. Different people like different things and react in different ways. Your best friend If you are writing for your best friend, they will probably use the same language as you do. So you might not have to think too much about the words you use! Old people Your grandfather might not understand all the words you use. For example, if you write 'that’s wicked', your grandfather might think you mean 'evil'. But you really meant 'cool'! Use more formal words and fewer chatty or slang words. This will help them understand your writing better. A foreigner If you are talking to someone who is learning to speak English, you should: Use clear language. Use simple sentences. This will help them not to get confused.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Identifying Your Purpose

content.topicNotes: Identifying your Purpose It's very important to identify your purpose before writing. Purpose You need to think about why you are writing. This will help you decide on the best form to use. This will help you decide on how your writing should look on the page. How your writing look on the page is called the layout. Writing to entertain people To entertain readers, add a lot of descriptions. To entertain readers, create an exciting atmosphere. Writing to inform people Imagine you are writing a non-fiction piece to inform people. You might need to use a more formal layout to help them understand. This might be a newspaper article or a formal letter. Writing to persuade people Imagine you are writing to persuade people. You will want to use lots of persuasive language. You will want to use words that show that you are making different points. like 'firstly...', 'secondly..., 'moreover...'

resources.title: Idiomatic Expressions

content.topicNotes: Idioms An idiom is an expression in a language that everyone understands but doesn’t make any literal sense. The words or ideas contained in them are hard to interpret unless someone explains them to you. How common are idioms? There are hundreds of examples of idioms used in English. The meaning of an idiom often cannot be understood from the literal meaning of the words used. This means that idioms have to be learned. Usually, we pick them up by listening to people use them in speech or by seeing them in books, adverts or on the internet. Why use idioms? Using an idiom in your writing can: Help to engage the reader. Add impact to your writing. Express a very specific meaning which is difficult to get across without an idiom. Idioms as metaphors Idioms are metaphors. They provide an alternative way of thinking about something, and their use makes our language interesting. Examples of Idioms Here are some examples of some common idiomatic expressions: ‘It’s raining cats and dogs’ This does NOT mean that cats and dogs are falling out of the sky! This means that it is raining very hard. 'It cost an arm and a leg' This does NOT mean that something cost two limbs to purchase! This means that something was extremely expensive. 'To get cold feet' This does NOT mean to have cold feet. This means to become nervous. For example, you could say 'I've got cold feet ahead of my wedding next week.' 'To kill two birds with one stone’ This does NOT mean to grab a stone, throw it and happen to kill two birds at once. This means to achieve two results in one action. ‘It was a blessing in disguise’ This means that even though the outcome initially seemed bad, something good came from it. 'She was over the moon' This does NOT mean that she was travelling in space! This means that she was extremely happy.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Language Techniques

resources.title: Impressions

content.topicNotes: Impressions What is an impression? An impression is a judgement that we make, based on clues from the text. Describing our impression of a character or setting is a type of inference. Clues to use for impressions We can use some clues from the text to form an impression of a character, such as: A character’s actions. A character’s words. A character’s appearance. How other characters describe them. More clues You can also find clues in how the author describes a setting. Another way to find clues is in the way different characters respond to a setting. Example Aunt Joy carries with her a strange scent of lavender, and =she always gives the best hugs=. The text gives the impression that Aunt Joy is friendly. We can infer that Aunt Joy is friendly because she 'always gives the best hugs'. Impressions: Another Example One impression Bare branches reached out from all angles, making the =dark and deserted= forest almost impenetrable. The creak of a swaying trunk sent a =shiver down her spine=. The text gives the impression that the forest was spooky because it is described as 'dark and deserted'. Another impression Bare branches reached out from all angles, making the =dark and deserted= forest almost impenetrable. The creak of a swaying trunk sent a =shiver down her spine=. The text gives the impression that the forest was spooky because the character felt 'a shiver down her spine'.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Comprehension

resources.title: In

content.topicNotes: In - In Words beginning with 'in' generally mean in or on. Invite To invite means to ask in. Example: Everyone thought Ruddy was being immature by not =inviting= Sally to the party. Alternative: Everyone thought Ruddy was being immature by not =asking= Sally to the party. Inside Inside means in something. Example: Strangely, it was warmer outside the house than =inside= the house! Alternative: Strangely, it was warmer outside the house than it was =in= the house! Intention An intention is something you aim to do. The 'tention' part of the word comes from the Latin word for stretching. So think of it like stretching towards (into) something. Example: Walter's =intentions= were admirable, despite what everyone thought. Alternative: Walter's =aims= were admirable, despite what everyone thought. Instinct An instinct is a natural response to something. The 'stinct' part of the word comes from the Latin word meaning to prick. So think of it like something pricking you towards ('into') a response. Example: When Stephen heard the car approaching, his first =instinct= was to run. Alternative: When Stephen heard the car approaching, his first =thought= was to run. In - In Words beginning with 'in' generally mean in or on. Include To include is to involve someone or something. You bring them 'in' to what you're doing. Example: Matthew wanted to make sure the new boy felt included in his friendship group, so he asked him to the park. Alternative: Matthew wanted to make sure the new boy felt involved in his friendship group, so he asked him to the park. Inverse The inverse is the opposite of something. The 'verse' part of the word comes from the Latin for 'turn'. So think of it like turning something 'on' itself. Example: Jack is popular, but his girlfriend has the inverse problem of being unpopular. Alternative: Jack is popular, but his girlfriend has the opposite problem of being unpopular. Invade To invade is to enter (go 'into') somewhere to take control. Example: The troops waited until dusk to invade the camp.Alternative: The troops waited until dusk to take control of the camp. Insight Insight is understanding of a problem or situation. If you have insight, you have 'sight' or wisdom 'into' a problem or situation. Example: The artists' work provided insight into the struggles of normal people during the war.Alternative: The artists' work helped people to understand the struggles of normal people during the war. In - In Words beginning with 'in' generally mean in or on. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'in': Invite Inside Invade Inter - Between Words beginning with 'inter' generally mean being among or between something. Intervene To intervene means to come or be between things. Example: Sally =intervened= to stop her friends from fighting. Alternative: Sally =went between= her friends to stop them from fighting. Example: In the =intervening= months, John worked at Waitrose. Alternative: In the months =between=, John worked at Waitrose. Intersect If two things intersect, they cross each other. Example: The roads =intersect= before the viewing point. Alternative: The roads =cross= before the viewing point. Interconnect Things that interconnect connect with each other. There is a connection 'between' them. Example: The two cities are =interconnected= by one long road. Alternative: The two cities are =connected= by one long road. International International means among nations, or involving more than one nation. Example: The =international= sporting event drew fans from across the world. Alternative: The =multi-nation= sporting event drew fans from across the world. Intermediate Intermediate means between two things. Example: He was =intermediate= level at chess. Alternative: He was =between beginner and advanced= level at chess.

resources.title: Indirect Speech

content.topicNotes: Indirect Speech Indirect speech is when you write what a person has said, but do not use the exact spoken words. Punctuation In indirect speech, you don’t use quotation marks or start a new line as you would for direct speech How to use indirect speech Below we include an example of how to convert direct speech into indirect speech: ‘I have no idea what I'm doing!’ said Rohit. Rohit did not know what he was doing. The second version above is an example of indirect speech. The purpose of this is to report on what was said. Why use indirect speech? We use indirect speech for a variety of reasons: Indirect speech is commonly used to describe speech that happened in the past, where you are repeating something that has been said to you before. The writer may not want to interrupt the flow of text with direct speech. It keeps the writer in a position of power, as what we read can be a second-hand interpretation of what was said. Examples of Indirect Speech Arya said she loved to swim. Joffrey said he was the king. Daenerys said she was bemused.

resources.title: Inference

content.topicNotes: Inference Definition Inference is making a clever guess or judgement. This guess or judgement is based on evidence from the text. Inference vs. retrieval Inference is different from retrieval. When we use inference, we will not find the exact information in the text. When we use inference, we will only find clues. Being asked to infer To know if you need to infer, look out for questions that begin with: 'What suggests that…?' 'How do you know that…?' 'How can you tell that…?' Other signs you need to infer You will need to use inference in these situations: When they ask us what a character might be thinking or feeling. When they ask us about the impression that we get about a character, setting or situation.

resources.title: Justifying Views
Justifying Your Views

content.topicNotes: Justifying Your Views Being able to justify your views with evidence from the text is important because it shows that you have understood what you have read. Good example What do you think is happening in this passage? 'He clasped the small square of paper so hard that it formed a concertina around his thumb. He had never received a better birthday present in all twelve years of his life. He knew the old man had heard him practising relentlessly, but to be recognised in this way made his chest tingle.' Bad example What do you think is happening in this passage? I think that the boy got a cinema ticket for his favourite film from his dad for his birthday. Good example answers I think that the boy has received an invitation to play in a music concert from an old man who heard how good he was while practising. I think it is a music concert because it says 'the old man had heard him practising relentlessly'. Another good answer I think it is important because the boy clasped the paper 'so hard' and felt his 'chest tingle'. Which suggests that he is excited, proud, and values the opportunity.'
