resources.title: Knot & Not

content.topicNotes: Knot and Not Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at some examples... Knot There is a knot in my shoelace. A knot is where pieces of string or other materials are tied up together. Not There are not enough crisps for us all. Not makes a sentence negative.

resources.title: Language Techniques
Less & Smaller

content.topicNotes: Min - Less Words beginning with 'min' generally mean something is less or smaller than something else. Minor The adjective minor means of less importance. From minor, we get the word minority, which means the smaller part or number of something. Example: Patrick missed his bus this morning, which was a =minor= inconvenience. Alternative: Patrick missed his bus this morning, which was a =small= inconvenience. Minuscule Minuscule means very small. Example: Chris must be hungry as his lunch was =minuscule=. Alternative: Chris must be hungry as his lunch was =tiny=. Minimum A minimum is the smallest amount possible. Example: Terry had very little motivation to exercise. He did the bare =minimum= to stay in shape. Alternative: Terry had very little motivation to exercise. He did the =least amount possible= to stay in shape. Minute Minute means very, very small. Example: The mouse was so =minute= we could hardly see it. Alternative: The mouse was so =tiny= we could hardly see it. National Minimum Wage The UK government brought in a national minimum wage in 1999. Minimum means the smallest amount possible, and the national minimum wage sets a limit on how little people of different age groups can be paid per hour. Micr - Small Words beginning with 'micr' generally mean something is small. Microscope A microscope lets us look at objects that are too small to look at with the naked eye. Things that are microscopic are technically so small that we can only see them with a microscope. We also use this word in everyday life to mean very, very small! Example: The dining hall serves food in =microscopic= portions! Alternative: The dining hall serves food in =minuscule= portions. Microorganism A microorganism is a microscopic organism - an organism we can only see under a microscope. Example: Bacteria, viruses and fungi are examples of microorganisms. Microeconomics Microeconomics looks at economics at an individual and business level. Microeconomics looks at the smaller picture compared to macroeconomics, which looks at the economy at a national level. Example: Troy was rubbish at microeconomics, but he passed his macroeconomics exam comfortably. Micromanage To micromanage is to manage every part of an operation or situation, no matter how small. Example: It was not his place to =micromanage= the office. Alternative: It was not his place to =manage every part= of the office. Microwave A microwave is a tiny electromagnetic wave. These kinds of waves can be used for cooking food. Unsurprisingly, microwave ovens cook food using microwaves. Example: Carris had bought a ready meal for dinner, forgetting that she did not own a microwave. Micr - Small Words beginning with 'micr' generally mean something is small. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'micr': Microscope Microorganism Microeconomics Micromanage Microwave

resources.title: Licence & License

content.topicNotes: Licence & License Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'licence' and 'license'. Licence Getting a drivers licence was very tricky. A licence is a permit. License We are not licensed to sell food. To be licensed is to be allowed, or to be permitted.

resources.title: Life & Earth

content.topicNotes: Bio - Life Words beginning with 'bio' generally mean something to do with life. Biography A biography is a detailed account of a person's life. An autobiography is when someone writes a detailed account of their own life. Example: Walter Isaacson wrote Steve Jobs' biography. Biology Biology is the scientific study of living organisms. Example: Stephen learnt about homeostasis by doing the Seneca GCSE biology course. Biometric Biometric means referring to measurements of and data on the body. Example: Biometric verification involves identifying people by some aspect of their body. Biomass Biomass means the overall mass of all living things in a specific area. In numerical terms, biomass is the total mass of living material in an organism multiplied by the number of organisms. Example: Pyramids of biomass are almost always pyramid-shaped. Biofuel Biofuel is fuel that comes from living things and waste from living things. Example: Biofuels are examples of renewable energy sources. Biodegrade To biodegrade means to be broken down by bacteria. Example: These plates are biodegradable, so they are more environmentally friendly than non-biodegradable plates. Geo - Earth Words beginning with 'geo' generally relate to the Earth. Geography Geography is effectively the study of the Earth. It's the study of the physical aspects of the Earth and human activity on Earth. Example: I learnt about volcanoes and earthquakes in my geography lesson today. Geology Geology is the study of rocks. Geology also refers to rocks that make up a particular area of the Earth. Example: Geology was always Isaac's favourite science. Geothermal Geothermal means connected to the Earth's inner heat. Example: The more Joan learnt about climate change, the more she thought about turning to geothermal energy. Geometry Geometry is a branch of mathematics. Geometry is concerned with space and the relationship between curves, points, lines etc. Example: Will passed his geometry exam with flying colours. Geospatial Geospatial means relating to data about the locations of particular features of the Earth's surface. The firm wanted to purchase new geospatial technology. Geo - Earth Words beginning with 'geo' generally relate to the Earth. Here are some examples of words beginning with 'geo': Geography Geology Geothermal Geometry Geospatial

resources.title: Literary Non-Fiction

content.topicNotes: Literary Non-Fiction Non-fiction relates to all writing based on facts. The term ‘literary’ links to the writer’s use of creative writing methods and styles that you would usually find in fiction stories too. Types of literary non-fiction Literary non-fiction can be written on a huge range of topics, as an essay or article. Travel writing is an important type of literary non-fiction. Travel writing uses creative language to help the reader imagine themselves in the place described. Essays are written formally to express a detailed view on a particular topic and balance facts. Writing methods Writers will carefully consider their tone when writing literary non-fiction and choose language that suits this tone. Literary non-fiction can use: Rhetorical (persuasive) non-fiction methods. Fiction methods that are usually used in narratives. Rhetorical methods Rhetorical methods may include: Statistics and facts Rhetorical questions Direct address Imperatives (command words) to motivate the reader to act Repetition
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Lover & Lacking

content.topicNotes: Phile - Lover Of Words ending in 'phile' generally mean a lover of something. Bibliophile A bibliophile is a lover of books. Example: Harris lived in the library because he was a =bibliophile=. Alternative: Harris lived in the library because he =loved books=. Oenophile An oenophile is a lover of wine. Example: Shirley was always at the pub because she was an =oenophile=. Alternative: Shirley was always at the pub because she =loved wine=. Technophile A technophile is a lover of technology. Example: Bertie studied computer science at university because he was a =technophile=. Alternative: Bertie studied computer science at university because he =loved technology=. Cinephile A cinephile is a lover of cinema. Example: Carris spends all her money on going to the cinema because she is a =cinephile=. Alternative: Carris spends all her money on going to the cinema because she =loves the cinema=. Phile - Lover Of Words ending in 'phile' generally mean a lover of something. Here are some examples of words that end in the suffix 'phile': Bibliophile Oenophile Technophile Cinephile Less - Without Words ending in 'less' generally mean without something. Worthless Worthless means without worth. Example: The car was =worthless= after the crash. Alternative: The car was =worth nothing= after the crash. Careless Careless means without care. Example: Ariel was so =careless= that she smashed a brand new bottle of wine. Alternative: Ariel =took so little care= that she smashed a brand new bottle of wine. Fearless Fearless means without fear. Example: Prince Philip was =fearless= when it came to slaying the dragon. Alternative: Prince Philip had =no fear= when it came to slaying the dragon. Homeless Homeless means without a home. Example: Quentin lost all his money gambling and become =homeless=. Alternative: Quentin lost all his money gambling and =lost his home= too. Reckless Reckless means not caring about the risks. Example: Walter could be =reckless= on his motorbike. Alternative: Walter could be =daring= on his motorbike. Less - Without Words ending in 'less' generally mean without something. Here are some examples of words ending in the suffix 'less': Worthless Careless Fearless Homeless Reckless

resources.title: Mail & Male

content.topicNotes: Mail and Male Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Mail Did you get my mail? Mail is another word for post. Male The new lion cub is a male. Male is the boy version of something (rather than the girl version or something!). You can have male people, male animals and so on. Types of Mail Mail is another word for post. Do not get the word 'mail' confused with the word 'male', which means the man version of something. These 2 words are homophones, which is why they sound the same. Let's look at different types of mail... Letter E-mail

resources.title: Main & Mane

content.topicNotes: Main and Mane Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Main The main part in the play went to Henry. Main means the most important. Mane The lion's mane was shimmering in the sun. A mane is the hair that horses, lions and some other animals have on their necks. Mane A mane is the hair that certain animals have on their necks. Some animals that have manes are... Lions Horses Unicorns

resources.title: Main & Subordinate Clauses

content.topicNotes: The Main Clause A clause is a string of words that contains a subject and a verb. Main clause A main clause is a clause that contains a subject, verb and an object. Main clauses make sense on their own. E.g. I like bananas.'I' is the subject. 'like' is the verb. 'bananas' is the object. A main clause is also known as an independent clause. Main clause examples I am a dog. I run home. I use Seneca. Main clause examples A main clause is a clause that contains a subject, verb and an object. Main clauses make sense on their own. I am a panda He loves chocolate The cat watched TV Subordinate Clause A subordinate clause is one that relies on a main clause to make sense. A subordinate clause is also known as a dependent clause. Subordinate clause A subordinate clause contains a subject and a verb and adds extra information to the sentence. E.g. I sat on a fence when I went to the park.The "when I went to the park" is the subordinate clause. Subordinate with main clause A subordinate clause needs to be attached to a main clause because it cannot make sense on its own. E.g. After she noticed it was missing… (What happened?) Subordinate clause examples A subordinate clause contains a subject and a verb and adds extra information to the sentence. Example one They watched me while I sang. Example two The audience clapped after the performance. Example three I do nothing during my lunchbreak.

resources.title: Making Your Writing Flow: Conjunctions

content.topicNotes: Making Your Writing Flow with Conjunctions You want your writing to 'flow' and not sound boring. We call this having cohesion. Conjunctions You could use conjunctions to help your writing flow. Conjunctions are joining words. Example without conjunctions Johnny is old. Johnny cannot walk very fast. Johnny is always late. These sentences sound very stop-start. But adding conjunctions makes the sentences flow a lot better... Example with conjunctions Johnny is old, so he cannot walk fast and is always late.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Making Your Writing Flow: Devices for Cohesion

content.topicNotes: Making Your Writing Flow with Nouns and Pronouns You want your writing to 'flow' and not sound boring. We call this having cohesion. Devices for cohesion Having cohesion is when your writing 'flow' and not sound boring. To make your writing flow, you can use a mixture of nouns and pronouns. Example without cohesion Gareth was a smart boy. Gareth always got the best grades. Gareth had lots of friends and Gareth was very sporty. Using 'Gareth' over and over again is very boring. If we use a mixture of pronouns and nouns, the sentences will flow more easily. Example with cohesion Gareth was a smart boy. He always got the best grades. Gareth had lots of friends and he was very sporty.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Making Your Writing Flow: Synonyms

content.topicNotes: Making Your Writing Flow with Synonyms You want your writing to 'flow' and not sound boring. We call this having cohesion. You could use synonyms to improve cohesion. Synonyms Synonyms are different words with the same meaning. Use synonyms to help your writing flow. Sentence without synonyms Jimmy is nice and he has a nice house. He likes to do nice things at the weekend. Using 'nice' again and again is very boring. Using synonyms for nice will make these sentences more interesting: Sentence with synonyms Jimmy is kind and he has a lovely house. He likes to do interesting things at the weekend.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: May

content.topicNotes: May Modal verbs are verbs that affect other verbs in sentences. 'May' is a modal verb. May 'May' is used to show how possible something is. Examples I may be late. You may play the guitar. More examples He may need to bring a change of clothes. They may feed the dog later on.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Modal Verbs

resources.title: Meat & Meet

content.topicNotes: Meat and Meet Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Meat Beef is a type of meat. Meat is the flesh of animals that we eat. Meet Where did you meet your friend? To meet means to come together with a person or a group of people. Meat Meat is the flesh of animals that we eat. Here are some different types of meat... Beef Lamb Pork

resources.title: Medal & Meddle

content.topicNotes: Medal and Meddle Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Medal She won a gold medal in gymnastics. A medal is a disc-shaped item you win in a competition. Meddle Don’t meddle in business that isn’t yours! To meddle is to get involved in something that you shouldn't get involved in!

resources.title: Might

content.topicNotes: Might Modal verbs are verbs that affect other verbs in sentences. 'Might' is a modal verb. Might 'Might' is used to show how possible something is. Examples I might not see you. He might get a fish. More examples He might have injured himself. He might wear a ghost costume.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Modal Verbs

resources.title: Missed & Mist

content.topicNotes: Missed and Mist Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Missed You missed your flight! Missed is the past tense of 'miss'. If you have missed something, you have either not hit it (like a target) or been too late for something (like a flight!). Mist The mist settled on the moors. Mist is fog. Things You Have Missed You have probably 'missed' lots of things in your life. The word 'missed' sounds like the word 'mist', which means fog. So do not get the words confused! Let's look at some times when you might have used the words 'missed'... I missed my train! I missed my flight! I missed my mother when I went away I missed the bus! I missed playing football when I was injured

resources.title: Modal Verbs
More Words Ending in '-cious' / '-tious'

content.topicNotes: Words Ending in '-cious' or '-tious' 'C' or 't'? We can determine whether to use a 'c' or a 't' by looking at the root word. If the word ends in '-ce', it will take the suffix '-cious'. If a word does not end in '-ce', it will use the suffix '-tious'. nutrition $$\leftrightarrow$$ nutritious There's one exception With the word 'anxiety' we use the suffix '-xious' anxiety $$\leftrightarrow$$ anxious Examples ambition → ambitious infection → infectious

resources.title: Morning & Mourning

content.topicNotes: Morning & Mourning Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'morning' and 'mourning'. Morning I eat toast every morning. Morning is the beginning of the day. Mourning The family wore black because they were in mourning. Mourning is showing sadness when someone dies.

resources.title: Must

content.topicNotes: Must Modal verbs are verbs that affect other verbs in sentences. 'Must' is a modal verb. Must 'Must' is used to show that something has to happen. Examples I must post that letter. Hattie must buy popcorn. More examples We must cook more dinners. We must not forget to feed Flossy.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Modal Verbs

resources.title: New & Alone

content.topicNotes: Nov - New Words containing 'nov' generally express the idea of newness. Novel Novel means new or different. Example: Hannah adopted a =novel= approach to her homework. Alternative: Hannah adopted a =new= approach to her homework. Innovate To innovate means to introduce change. Example: The business had to close down because it failed to =innovate=. Alternative: The business had to close down because it failed to =introduce new change=. Novice A novice is a new or inexperienced person. Example: Jasper could only do basic tasks at work because he was a =novice= at computing. Alternative: Jasper could only do basic tasks at work because he was =inexperienced= in computing. Renovate To renovate is to make something like new again. Example: The couple were desperate to =renovate= their old house. Alternative: The couple were desperate to =refresh= their old house. Sol - Alone Words containing 'sol' generally mean being alone. Isolate To isolate is to separate something from other things. Example: Dylan was lonely because he had =isolated= himself from all of his friends. Alternative: Dylan was lonely because he had =separated= himself from all of his friends. Desolate Desolate means empty, lacking or lonely. Example: The house stood in a =desolate= field. Alternative: The house stood in an =empty= field. Solo A solo act is something done by one person. Example: Thomas preferred singing =solo=. Alternative: Thomas preferred singing =alone=. Solitude Solitude is the state of being alone. Example: As Ricky got older, he increasingly enjoyed =solitude=. Alternative: As Ricky got older, he increasingly enjoyed =being alone=. Solitary Solitary means existing alone or doing alone. Example: Scrooge led a =solitary= life. Alternative: Scrooge led a =lonely= life. Sol - Alone Words containing 'sol' generally mean being alone. Here are some examples of words containing the root 'sol': Isolate Desolate Solo Scrooge In Dickens' A Christmas Carol, Scrooge chooses to isolate himself from people at the start of the story. He enjoys __sol__itude and living a __sol__itary life. All the words containing 'sol' relate to being alone.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Common Word Roots

resources.title: Newspaper Articles

content.topicNotes: Newspaper Articles Newspaper articles can be information articles that provide facts about recent news and events, or opinion articles that express the perspective of the writer about a particular topic. Information news articles Information news articles have been written since ancient Rome when information was carved into stone and put in a public place. Information news articles are written to give factual information about current news and events. Information news articles give information about the 5 Ws: Who, What, Where, When, and Why. Broadsheet newspapers The style of an information news article changes based on whether the newspaper is a broadsheet or tabloid newspaper. Broadsheet newspapers are more formal and are seen as more serious. Broadsheet newspapers include longer, more in-depth articles with lots of factual information. Tabloid newspapers Tabloid newspapers are read more for entertainment. Tabloid newspapers include less text and more photographs. Tabloid newspapers use many ‘puns’ (a play on words) in headlines to grab the reader’s attention.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Not & 'Inter-'

content.topicNotes: Ways of Saying 'Not" Prefixes are letters or words placed at the start of words which change their meaning. The prefix 'in-' means 'not'. Let's look at some rules for using the prefix 'in'... ‘In-’ ‘In-’ means ‘not’. For example: __In__active - =not= active. __In__correct - =not= correct. __In__sane - =not= sane. 'Il-' But a word starting ‘l’ will become ‘-il’ (instead of –in). For example: __Il__legal - =not= legal. __Il__legible - =not= legible or readable. 'Im-' If a word starts with ‘m’ or 'p', use '–im' (instead of –in). For example: __Im__mature - =not= mature. __Im__perfect - =not= perfect. 'Ir-' If a root word starts with ‘r’, use ‘ir’ (instead of – in). For example: __Ir__regular - =not= regular. __Ir__responsible - =not= responsible. Inactive Inactive means =not= being active. Insane Insane means =not= sane. Sane means having a normal mind. Incorrect Incorrect means =not= correct. 'Inter-' Means Between or Among Prefixes are letters or words placed at the start of words which change their meaning. The prefix 'inter-' means 'between' or 'among'. Let's look at some words beginning with 'inter'... __Inter__city Intercity means travelling =between= cities. For example, an intercity train goes between cities. __Inter__national Something that is international involves more than one nation. So something '=between=' or '=among=' nations. For example, an international sporting competition is between different countries. Interval An interval is a time period =between= things. For example, an interval between acts at the theatre. Interact To interact means to talk =among= people. International The prefix inter means between or among. Something that is international involves more than one nation. So something '=between=' or '=among=' nations. Interview An interview is a meeting between people. Intervene Bart is intervening in the fight. To intervene means to get involved in something.

resources.title: Noting Down Ideas

content.topicNotes: Noting Down Your Ideas You should note down your original ideas, which you can then develop upon. Sometimes, this means doing some extra reading and research! Writing a love story First, you should write the initial idea down. A girl Sally falls in love with a boy named Timmy. Then, you can think about: Where Sally and Timmy meet. How Sally and Timmy meet. How Sally and Timmy fall in love. If there are any problems on the way to falling in love. Writing an action story First, you should write the initial idea down. You want to end your story with a car chase. Then, you can think about: What characters are involved. What led to the car chase. Writing a horror story First, you should write the initial idea down. The story will start with a murder. Then, you can think about: Who was murdered. Why the murder took place. If the mystery of the murder will be solved.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Nouns

content.topicNotes: Nouns You need to know the following key terms: Noun A person, place, thing, feeling or idea. E.g. London, mum, cat, table, happiness. Abstract noun An idea or concept - something that you cannot actually see, touch, hear, smell or taste. The opposite of a concrete noun. E.g. Love, hatred, anger, happiness, truth, freedom, dedication, peace, knowledge. Collective noun A group of nouns. E.g. Team, army, family, group, audience, herd. Common noun All nouns are either common nouns or proper nouns. Common nouns are places, things, feelings or ideas. E.g. Home, school, book, computer, trees, television. Concrete noun A thing (noun) that can be touched, tasted, heard, seen, or smelled. The opposite of an abstract noun. E.g. Dog, building, tree, fire, water. Pronoun A word used to replace a noun. We use pronouns so we don't need to repeat the same nouns over and over again. E.g. I, you, he, she, it, we, they, me. Proper noun All nouns are either common nouns or proper nouns. Proper nouns are the names of specific people or places. E.g. Kate, Harry, Liverpool, England, BBC. Concrete Nouns A concrete noun is a thing that can be touched, tasted, heard, seen, or smelled. Here are some examples... Dog Cat Chair Book Gun Collective Nouns A collective noun is a group of nouns. Here are some examples: Army Choir Family Swarm

resources.title: Numbers

content.topicNotes: Bi - Two Words beginning with 'bi' generally mean two of something. Bilingual A person who is bilingual speaks two languages fluently. Example: Jenny's mother is Spanish and her father is Italian. She is =bilingual= because her parents taught her both Spanish and Italian. Alternative: Jenny's mother is Spanish and her father is Italian. She is =fluent in two languages= because her parents taught her both Spanish and Italian. Bicycle A bicycle is a cycle with two wheels. Example: Johnny prefers riding his =bicycle= to taking the bus. Alternative: Johnny prefers riding his =two-wheeled cycle= to taking the bus. Binary Binary means involving two things or having two parts. In maths and science, a binary system only has two numbers - one and zero. Example: Sapphire had to make a difficult =binary= decision - should she stay or should she go? Alternative: Sapphire had to decide between =two options= - should she stay or should she go? Biform Biform means having two forms. Example: A Minotaur is a =biform= creature: half bull, half man. Alternative: A Minotaur is a =two-form= creature: half bull, half man. Bipolar Bipolar disorder affects a person's mood. Sufferers alternate between two states: depression (feeling very down) and mania (feeling very happy). Example: It's thought that around 3% of Americans suffer from bipolar disorder. Bi - Two Words beginning with 'bi' generally mean two of something. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'bi': Bilingual Bicycle Binary (system) Tri - Three Words beginning with 'tri' generally mean three of something. Triathlon A triathlon is a competition involving three different sporting events - normally swimming, cycling and running. Tricycle A tricycle is a cycle with three wheels. Tripod A tripod is a stand with three legs. Tri - Three Words beginning with 'tri' generally mean three of something. Here are some examples of words beginning with the prefix 'tri': Triathlon Tricycle Tripod Triangle

resources.title: Object of a Sentence

content.topicNotes: Identifying the Object The object of a sentence is the noun or pronoun that receives the action carried out by the subject. The object can also tell us who or what the subject does something to. Spotting the object In the sentence ‘John ate cake’, ‘cake’ is the object. 'Cake' is the noun that receives John’s action of eating. In the sentence, ‘you understand English’, 'English' is the object. 'English' is the thing that has affected the subject. Spotting the object 2 To help identify the object, ask yourself who or what the subject is doing the action to. Direct objects A direct object is a type of object. The direct object is the noun directly receiving the action of the verb. E.g. in ‘John ate cake’, 'cake' is the direct object. 'Cake' is the thing that the subject is eating (doing). Indirect objects The other type of object is an indirect object. The indirect object tells can tell us: Who or what the noun is that benefits from the action. Who or what the noun is that is the goal of the action. E.g. In ‘John gave the cake to me’, 'me' is the indirect object because 'me' is who benefits from the verb (gave). Sentence formation Sometimes the indirect object goes before the direct object. E.g. ‘John gave Mary some flowers’. ‘Flowers’ are the direct object because 'flowers is the object being given. 'Mary' is the indirect object because she is the one who receives the object.

resources.title: Opinion News Articles

content.topicNotes: Opinion News Articles Opinion news articles present the writer’s perspective (point of view). Rhetorical methods Opinion news articles often include rhetorical (persuasive) methods. Opinion news articles often include a strong tone to highlight the writer’s thoughts and feelings on a particular topic. Facts When reading news articles, it is important to be able to tell between what is a fact and what is an opinion. A fact can be proven to be correct, such as a statistic or research. Opinions An opinion is a thought or belief that a person has that cannot be proved. Opinions don’t always have to begin with phrases like ‘I think…’ or ‘I feel…’. Sometimes opinions may be less obvious. Opinion articles are usually ‘biased’ (one-sided) because the writer will often only express their personal opinion and not provide the other point of view. Biased Opinion articles are usually ‘biased’ (one-sided). Biased means that the writer only expresses their personal opinion and does not provide the other point of view.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Over & Under

content.topicNotes: Sub - Below Words beginning with 'sub' generally mean below. Substandard Substandard means below standard. Example: Mrs Jones thoughts Pascal's work was =substandard=. Alternative: Mrs Jones thought Pascal's work was =dissatisfactory=. Submerge To submerge means to go completely below the surface of water. So to be submerged means to be completely covered by water. Example: The diver took one long breath before =submerging=. Alternative: The diver took one long breath before =going under=. Subject A subject is someone or something that's being discussed or considered. So think of a subject like someone or something being 'under' the watch of others. A subject is also someone 'under' a ruler. Example: The King addressed his =subjects= from his balcony. Alternative: The King addressed his =people= from his balcony. Subconscious Subconscious means relating to the part of the mind that we are not fully aware of - the part of the mind that's 'below' our consciousness. Example: Bridget had a =subconscious= fear of failing. Alternative: Bridget had a fear of failing that she was =not completely aware of=. Submerging Submarines A submarine submerges. That's why its name begins with the prefix 'sub' - it's a ship designed to go below the surface of the water. Super - Above Words beginning with 'super' generally mean above or beyond. Supernormal Supernormal means beyond normal. Example: The Incredibles have =supernormal= powers. Alternative: The Incredibles have powers =beyond normal humans=. Supersonic Supersonic means quicker than the speed of sound. Example: Concorde could travel at =supersonic= speeds. Alternative: Concorde could travel =faster than the speed of sound=. Superscript A superscript is a number, letter or word that is written above another character. Example: In the equation 32 = 9, 2 is a superscript.

resources.title: Paragraphs

content.topicNotes: Paragraphs You need to be able to write in paragraphs. Structure of paragraphs Generally, each paragraph in a piece of writing contains one key point. Writers often start paragraphs with hooks, which encourage readers to think about the main point of the paragraph. The topic sentence is where a writer introduces their main point. Writers will then expand on these sentences with evidence and examples. Writers may end by leading into the following paragraph. Paragraph length The length of a paragraph can be significant. For example: A writer may use a long paragraph to build up a detailed description of a setting. A writer may use a one-sentence paragraph to emphasise a rhetorical question or emphasise a point. When to begin a new paragraph You need to start a new paragraph when: Location changes. Time changes. The action changes. You introduce a new idea or character. Someone starts speaking. When you are using dialogue, you need to start a new paragraph every time you change speaker.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Text Structure

resources.title: Participle Clauses

content.topicNotes: Participles Participles are verb forms that don’t express tense. In other words, participles don’t tell you if the verb is in the past, present or future tense. Types of participle There are 2 types of participle: The present participle which always ends in ‘ing’. The past participle which normally ends in ‘ed’ (unless it’s an irregular verb). Present participles Present participles are verbs that don’t express tense and end in ‘ing’. E.g. In ‘running on the beach, I felt great’, 'running' is the present participle. The word 'running' doesn’t tell you when the action is taking place but 'running' is still an action. Past participles The past participle normally ends in ‘ed’ (unless it’s an irregular verb). E.g. In ‘excited to be voted in, Elizabeth jumped for joy’, 'excited' is the past participle. The word 'excited' doesn’t tell us when it happened but it is still a verb. Irregular past participles The past participle normally ends in ‘ed’ (unless it’s an irregular verb). E.g. In ‘broken by the exam, Simon cried’, 'broken' is the past participle. The word 'broken' doesn’t tell us when the action happened but it is still an action. Participle phrases A phrase contains a verb, or a subject, but NOT both. Phrases CANNOT stand alone as a sentence. A complete sentence needs to have a main clause (subject and verb). Participle phrases are phrases that contain Participle verbs. But no subject. E.g. 'Understanding the game was over, Simon dropped to the ground.’

resources.title: Passive Voice

content.topicNotes: The Passive Voice The passive voice is when the subject of the sentence is having the action done to them. Let's look at some examples of sentences using the passive voice. The goat (subject) is being carried The horse (subject) is being ridden The book (subject) is being read The food (subject) is being eaten The rabbit (subject) is being brushed

resources.title: Past & Passed

content.topicNotes: Past & Passed Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'past' and 'passed'. Past In the past, there were no computers. The past is a time that has happened already. Passed She passed me on the street. Passed is the past tense of pass, which means to go in front of or before someone or thing.

resources.title: Peace & Piece

content.topicNotes: Peace and Piece Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Peace The teacher just wanted some peace and quiet. In the example above, peace means not being disturbed by anything. Peace can also mean being free from war or violence. Piece There is a piece of chocolate cake left. Piece means a part of something. Things in Pieces A piece is a part of something. The word 'piece' sounds like the word 'peace', which means not being disturbed. Do not confuse these two words! Let's look at some common 'pieces'... Jigsaw =pieces= =Piece= of apple pie =Pieces= of cheesecake Chess =pieces=

resources.title: People

content.topicNotes: Er - One Who Words ending in 'er' generally mean someone who does that thing. Trainer A trainer is someone who trains. Example: Mohammad is a dog =trainer=. Alternative: Mohammad =trains= dogs. Manager A manager is someone who manages. Example: Eric is my =manager= at work. Alternative: Eric is my =boss= at work. Publisher A publisher is an individual or company that publishes books - prepares them to go on sale. Example: Rosie could not get her book to launch because no =publishers= liked it. Alternative: Rosie could not get her book to launch because no one in the =publishing industry= liked it. Teacher A teacher is someone who teaches. Example: Sacha was a =teacher= of philosophy. Alternative: Sacha =taught= philosophy. Baker A baker is someone who bakes. Example: Duncan was an excellent =baker= but a rubbish cook. Alternative: Duncan =could bake= excellently but he was a rubbish cook. Er - One Who Words ending in 'er' generally mean someone who does that thing. Here are some examples of words ending in the suffix 'er': Trainer Manager Publisher Teacher Baker Mary Berry the Baker Mary Berry is a professional baker. She has the title 'baker' because she is someone who ('-er') bakes. Gareth Southgate Gareth Southgate is a football manager. He has this title because he is someone who ('-er') manages a football team. Teachers A teacher is someone who ('-er') teaches. Here are some examples of famous 'teachers': Cameron Diaz (Bad Teacher) Jack Black (School of Rock) Miss Trunchbull (Matilda) Ist - Someone Who Words ending in 'ist' generally mean someone does the thing coming before the 'ist'. Chemist A chemist studies chemistry or works with chemicals. Example: Hugo was a third-year chemist at Oxford University. Scientist A scientist studies science or works in the field of science. Example: Lesley is a scientist who specialises in marine biology. Capitalist A capitalist is someone who follows or believes in capitalism. Capitalism is a political system in which private owners own all industry. Example: The USA is a capitalist country. Communist A communist is someone who follows or believes in communism. Communism is the belief that the state should own all industry and there should be no social classes. Example: China is a communist country. Ist - Someone Who Words ending in 'ist' generally mean someone does the thing coming before the 'ist'. Here are some examples of words ending in the suffix 'ist': Chemist Scientist Capitalist Communist

resources.title: Personal & Formal Letters

content.topicNotes: Personal and Formal Letters Letters are written to communicate messages, thoughts and feelings to another individual person or group of people. Letters can be either formal or informal. Salutation Letters begin with a salutation. Salutation is a greeting. Salutation is different depending if the letter is formal or informal. Formal salutations include ‘Dear...’, ‘Greetings...’ or ‘To whom it may concern’ if the person writing does not know the name of the person who will receive the letter. Informal salutations include ‘Hi...’, ‘Hello...’ or ‘To...’. Paragraphs Ideas in letters are organised in paragraphs that separate different topics or time periods. Letters often include a recount of past events and experiences and the writer’s thoughts and feelings. Sign-off Letters end with a sign-off. Formal examples of sign-off include: ‘Yours sincerely’ if you know the person you are writing to. ‘Yours faithfully’ if you do not know the recipient (person receiving) of the letter. Informal examples include ‘Love’ or ‘Best wishes’. Historical communication Just like diaries, personal letters are usually kept private between the writer and recipient of the letter. Sometimes letters can be published if they document important historical communication.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Formats

resources.title: Phrasal Verbs
Phrasal Verbs

content.topicNotes: Separable Phrasal Verbs Phrasal verbs are idiomatic expressions. Phrasal verbs are created by combining verbs and prepositions to make new verbs. The meaning is often not obvious from the definitions of each word. Use of phrasal verbs Phrasal verbs are used in both written and spoken English. New examples are formed all the time, as they are a flexible way of creating new terms. Separable phrasal verbs Separable phrasal verbs can be separated into two parts in a sentence. The phrasal verb doesn’t have to be separated, but it can be: E.g. ‘Take back’In the sentence ‘I had to take the shirt back to the shop because it was too large’, the verb ‘take’ is able to be separated from the proposition ‘back’. Separable phrasal verbs examples Other examples of separable phrasal verbs include: Write down - 'write your ideas down'. Put on - 'Put your hat on'. Blow up - 'Can you blow those balloons up?'. Fill up - 'Fill the car up'. Find out - 'Find it out for me'. Hand in - 'Hand your homework in'. Examples of Separable Phrasal Verbs E.g. 'take out' 'Jake, can you take the bins out?' E.g. 'throw away' 'Are you going to throw that food away'. Inseparable Phrasal Verbs Phrasal verbs are idiomatic expressions. Phrasal verbs are created by combining verbs and prepositions to make new verbs. The meaning is often not obvious from the definitions of each word. Inseparable phrasal verbs Inseparable examples of phrasal verbs must stay together in a sentence: E.g. ‘Come over’In the sentence ‘Anya, please come over to my house', you can’t separate 'come' and 'over'. Inseparable examples There are fewer examples of inseparable phrasal verbs. Some examples of phrasal verbs are: Look after. Jump to. Look on. Stand by. Run across. Wait on. Two prepositions Sometimes you can have two prepositions in the phrasal verb. For example: Check up on. Get along with. Drop out of. Keep up with. Get rid of. Examples of Inseparable Phrasal Verbs E.g. 'run across' 'I wish I could run across the field.' E.g. 'go through' 'It's time to go through your homework.'
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Phrasal Verbs

resources.title: Plain & Plane

content.topicNotes: Plain and Plane Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Plain I like plain rice. Something that is plain is not decorated and has not had anything added to it. Plane You need to go on a plane to get to Italy. A plane is a vehicle that travels in the air. Types of Planes A plane is a vehicle designed to travel in the air. There are many different types of planes. Let's look at some examples... Aeroplane Propeller plane Helicopter

resources.title: Poems Structure

content.topicNotes: Poems Structure Some forms of poems have a common structure, for example, sonnets or haiku poems. Sonnets Sonnets are 14-line poems that are usually written about love. Shakespeare wrote many of such sonnets. Haiku Haiku poems originated in Japan and always have three lines. Haiku poems also have the same number of syllables in each line - five in the first line, seven in the second line, and five in the third line. Rhyme Poems do not always have to rhyme. Sometimes poets will include a regular rhyme scheme, for example, AABB or ABAB (A lines rhyme, and B lines rhyme). Sometimes poets will include no clear rhyme scheme at all.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing formats

resources.title: Poetry

content.topicNotes: Poetry A poem is usually a short literature text on a particular topic and theme. Poems can be based on a story, event, or different thoughts and feelings. Autobiographical & persona poems Poems can be autobiographical or based on a fictional persona. Autobiographical poems are based on the poet’s own experiences and emotions. Persona poems are about a fictional person and their experiences and emotions. Stanzas Poems can be separated into different stanzas (sections) similar to paragraphs. There is no single way to structure a poem - sometimes poets may choose to have lots of stanzas or none. Calligrams Some poems have a shape that reflects the topic of the poem, called ‘calligrams’. For example, a poem about the beauty of a rainbow could be in the shape of a rainbow.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing formats

resources.title: Practice & Practise

content.topicNotes: Practice & Practise Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'practice' and 'pracrise'. Practice The energy department tried to make their practice more efficient. Practice is a noun that describes something done routinely (e.g. a medical practice). Practise He started to practise golf before he could walk. To practise is a verb, meaning to do something repeatedly.

resources.title: Prediction

content.topicNotes: Prediction Prediction in reading is making a clever guess about what might happen next in a text. The predictions should be based on what you know so far from the text. Being asked to predict We need to make a prediction when we're asked what we think will happen next! Answering a prediction question It is important to go through the text and highlight key information about characters. Key information about the character includes: the character's personality the character's appearance the character's actions Key information Other key information would be: the location the feel/atmosphere of the setting the plot (key events so far) Using the key information Then we can make a prediction about what might happen next. Based on the key information we know so far.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Comprehension

resources.title: Prediction Practice

content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Comprehension

resources.title: Predictions: Example

content.topicNotes: Prediction: Example In a prediction, we need to be able to justify why we think something will happen, using evidence from the text. Text 'The old woman longed for the drought to end. As she looked over the hills, a bank of dark, ominous clouds drew in and a cold breeze disturbed the dry, thirsty trees.' Prediction From the text, we could predict that a rainstorm will come and end the drought. We could also predict that the old woman will live happily. Why? We can predict that the rainstorm will come. Because we know that dark clouds tend to mean that rain is coming. We can predict that the old woman will live happily. Because we know that the old woman wanted the drought to be over. What can we not predict? We could not predict that the old woman will find a precious emerald in the dirt and become rich. We can't predict this because there is nothing in the text to suggest that this might happen!
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Reading > Reading Comprehension

resources.title: Prefixes
Prepositions

content.topicNotes: Types of Preposition Prepositions help us to imagine a scene with greater accuracy. Choosing the right preposition makes a big difference to the meaning of a sentence. Prepositions describing location Prepositions relating to location show the relationship of a noun or pronoun to another word. Examples include: under/over above/below near/close to inside/outside opposite/beside on/in Prepositions relating to time Prepositions relating to time show the relationship of a noun or pronoun to another word. Examples include: at midnight on Thursday in two months Prepositions about direction Prepositions relating to direction show the relationship of a noun or pronoun to another word. Examples include: through the field towards the beach into the ocean Prepositional Phrases When we think of the noun or pronoun connected to the preposition as one thing, we call it a ‘prepositional phrase’. ‘He lived near the ocean' In this sentence, the words near the ocean make a prepositional phrase. ‘He slept under the warm blanket’ In this sentence, the words under the warm blanket make a prepositional phrase. 'She hid beneath the table’ In this sentence, the words beneath the table make a prepositional phrase.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Word Classes

resources.title: Principal & Principle

content.topicNotes: Principal & Principle Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'principal' and 'principle'. Principal The principal motivation was to win. Principal means most important (the principal role in a play, the principal of a school) Principle She lived by her principles. A principle is a belief or a truth.

resources.title: Profit & Prophet

content.topicNotes: Profit & Prophet Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. For example, 'profit' and 'prophet'. Profit The company made a great profit in their first year. A profit is the money or financial gain made by selling, exchanging or doing business. Prophet She looked to the prophet to explain what might happen. A prophet is a religious teacher, or someone who is believed to tell the future.

resources.title: Pronouns

content.topicNotes: Pronouns Pronouns are words we can use to replace nouns. Here are some examples of pronouns: It He She They Using Nouns and Pronouns You want your writing to 'flow' and not sound boring. Your writing will sound boring if you repeat words too often! Changing whether you use a noun or a pronoun can help to make your writing more exciting. Boring example Read this paragraph: Leo was a cat. Leo liked to go hunting. When Leo went hunting he liked to find mice. Leo enjoyed catching mice because they were a challenge. The mice knew Leo was looking for them, and often hid. Don't you think the paragraph sounds boring? This is because the person writing it has used the name 'Leo' over and over again. Now let's look at a more interesting example... More interesting example Here is a more interesting version: Leo was a cat who liked to go hunting. When he went hunting he liked to find mice. He enjoyed catching them because they were a challenge. The mice knew Leo was looking for them, and often hid. As you can see, using a mixture of nouns (Leo) and pronouns (he) makes this paragraph 'flow' more easily. It is easier and nicer to read!
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > SPaG > Word Classes

resources.title: Proof Reading: Punctuation, Spelling & Grammar

content.topicNotes: Proofreading Proofreading is when you check your work for mistakes after you have finished. After writing, you need to check your punctuation. Proofreading for punctuation It is easy to make a mistake with your punctuation. You need to proofread your work when you've finished. This means you should check for errors in your punctuation. Where can there be errors? You should check for mistakes in: commas, hyphens, capital letters, full stops, colons, semicolons, etc. Proofreading for spelling It is easy to make a mistake with your spelling sometimes. You need to proofread your work when you've finished. This will help you spot any spelling mistakes. Proofreading for grammar It is easy to make a mistake with your grammar sometimes. You need to proofread your work when you've finished. This will help you find errors in your grammar. What to check in grammar You should make sure the tenses of your verbs are consistent. You should make sure you use the correct subjects for your verbs. And other things too!
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Proof Reading: Steps

content.topicNotes: Proofreading Proofreading is one of the most important steps when writing. Everyone makes mistakes! Proofreading is when you check your work for mistakes after you have finished. Steps for proofreading Read your work out loud to help you spot errors. Read your writing word by word to help you spot mistakes. Try reading your work looking for one type of error you're likely to make. For example: spelling, punctuation, grammar, etc. How to proofread It is vital that you proofread your work after you have written it. This helps to reduce the chance of mistakes. You should proofread your work for punctuation, spelling and grammar.
content.description: English: GCSE Groundwork > Writing > Writing Composition

resources.title: Punctuation
Qualifiers & Quantifiers

content.topicNotes: Qualifiers Qualifiers are words that are usually used before adjectives or adverbs. Adjectives and adverbs are examples of modifiers. Qualifiers either limit, weaken or strengthen the modifier’s meaning. Examples of qualifiers The qualifier 'hardly' in the phrase ‘hardly a big monster’ is used as a qualifier to weaken the adjective 'big'. The qualifier 'very' in the phrase ‘a very big monster’ is used to strengthen the adjective 'big'. Spotting a qualifier Look at the difference between these three sentences: He is a handsome man. He is a somewhat handsome man. He is a really handsome man. All sentences give you information about the man’s handsomeness. Spotting a qualifier 2 'He is a somewhat handsome man' weakens the handsomeness of the man. 'He is a really handsome man' strengthens the handsomeness of the man. 'Somewhat' and 'really' are qualifiers in these sentences. Categories of qualifiers There are four different categories of qualifiers: Qualifiers of time - usually, always, never, sometimes, etc. Qualifiers of quantity - some, most, all, none, etc. Qualifiers of certainty - I guess, I think, I know, I am certain, etc. Qualifiers of possibility - could, may, likely, possible, probable, etc. Using Qualifiers Qualifiers either limit, weaken or strengthen the meaning of an adjective or adverb. I am really cold I never go to the beach I know I can bake a good cake I am never doing that again I __always __ enjoy a good wash Quantifiers Quantifiers tell us something about the amount or quantity of something (a noun). Quantifiers can tell you about how many of something we have. Quantifiers as numbers Numbers as quantifiers: I have 3 apples. I have hundreds of apples. The number '3' and 'hundreds' are both quantifiers. Quantifiers as words Quantifiers can also tell us about how much of something we have: I have most of the apples. I have __lots __ of apples. I have __plenty __ of apples. I have no apples. 'Most', 'lots', 'plenty' and 'no' are all quantifiers.

resources.title: Question Marks & Exclamation Marks

content.topicNotes: Question Marks and Exclamation Marks Both question and exclamation marks are commonly used at the end of sentences. Question Marks Question marks are used to show that a question is being asked. E.g. Why haven't you done your homework? Question marks are not used at the end of sentences with indirect questions: E.g. The teacher asked Selena whether she had done her homework. Exclamation Marks Exclamation marks are used at the end of sentences to add emphasis. Exclamation marks are used to indicate strong emotions (like surprise, passion, excitement or anger). Exclamation marks can also be used to indicate abrupt shouting or interjections. For example: Hey! Give me back my pencil! I'm so happy to see you! That was the most incredible match! Question Mark and Exclamation Mark Examples Question marks What does the British flag look like again? What colours are in the British flag? Why can't I remember the British flag? Exclamation marks Your dancing is amazing! Wow! I wish I could dance like you. That is incredible!

A rein is a piece of material that someone uses to control a horse. Rain, Reign and Rein Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... resources.title: Relative Clauses

content.topicNotes: Relative Pronouns Relative pronouns are words used to introduce relative clauses. Relative clauses are used to add extra information to a sentence. Let's look at some examples of common relative pronouns... Who When Where Whose Which That Relative Clauses A relative clause is used to add extra information to a sentence. We use relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. Let's look at how you use relative clauses... Relative clause example Here is a simple sentence: The witch tricked the children. To add more information, we can add a relative clause using the relative pronoun ‘who’. The witch, who lived in a gingerbread house, tricked the children. Let's look at some other examples on the next slides... Relative clause using when I am going to visit my friend in New York when I have enough money saved. resources.title: Retrieval

content.topicNotes: Questions Asking to Retrieve Information from Text What is retrieving? Retrieving means getting or fetching something. This is like a retriever dog that fetches things for its owner. Retrieval questions ask you to get information directly from the text. Retrieving information You need to be able to spot questions that are asking you to retrieve information directly from the text. Look for hints in the question to know when you need to retrieve information directly from the text. Questions asking to retrieve To know if a question ask you to retrieve, look out for questions that: Begin with 'In the text…'. Begin with 'According to the text...'. Atention! You also need to retrieve information directly from the text when a question begins with: 'who', 'what', 'where', 'why', 'when' or 'how' Where did the cat find its dinner?

resources.title: Run-on Sentences

content.topicNotes: Run-on Sentences Sometimes you will just join multiple sentences together using conjunctions to create a run-on sentence. You should NOT use run-on sentences because they are bad for your writing style. Run-on sentence example ‘John likes swimming and he likes fish and he also likes to sit on the sand and then he likes to get an ice-cream and then he calls his friend and he….’ Run-on sentences are bad Run-on sentences don’t apply boundaries to any of the ideas in writing. The lack of boundaries in run-on sentences makes it difficult for the reader. Run-on sentences are difficult for the reader because all the ideas have to be processed at once. Avoiding run-on sentences Think of each idea separately. Apply boundaries to individual sections of your writing by using punctuation. If in doubt, apply a full stop after each idea you present. Run-on Sentences Run-on sentences use conjunctions to join multiple sentences together. You should avoid using run-on sentences because they are hard to read. Run-on sentence example An example of a run-on sentence is below. The run-on sentence is very difficult to read! 'I went to the shop and it was very cold so I bought some gloves which were very warm and fuzzy and when I put them on I found that they were soft inside which meant that my hands were comfortable and warm and it meant I could get on with the jobs I had to do that day by...' Easier to read The sentence below is much easier to read. The sentence contains exactly the same information as before: 'I went to the shop and it was very cold. I decided I needed some warm and fuzzy gloves. The gloves were so soft inside. My hands were comfortable and warm in the gloves. The gloves allowed me to complete all the jobs I had to do that day.'

resources.title: SPaG
Saving

content.topicNotes: Serv - Save Words containing 'serv' generally express the idea of saving. Preserve To preserve is to keep or try to keep something in its present state. Example: Ollie tried to =preserve= the cake by storing it in a cake tin. Alternative: Ollie tried to =keep the cake fresh= by storing it in a cake tin. Conserve To conserve means to save and protect something. Example: Rosie didn't go to the party to =conserve= her energy for the running race. Alternative: Rosie didn't go to the party to =save= her energy for the running race. Reserve To reserve is to save something for a set purpose. Example: Ross called the restaurant to =reserve= a table for his date. Alternative: Ross called the restaurant to =save= a table for his date. Preservation in Ancient Egypt The Ancient Egyptians used to bandage mummies for a number of reasons. One reason was to try and preserve the dead bodies (remember that to preserve means to try and keep something in it's present state!).

resources.title: Saying How & Why

content.topicNotes: Using Fronted Adverbials to Describe How Fronted adverbials are words or phrases at the start of a sentence that add extra detail. We can use fronted adverbials to show how something has happened. We call these fronted adverbials of manner. Let's look at some examples... Quickly... Quickly, the mouse ran away. Slowly Slowly, I made my way to school. Lovingly... Lovingly, my father hugged me. As... As fast as he could, the man ran away. Like... Like a stealthy snake, he slid away. Using Fronted Adverbials to Show How Fronted adverbials are words or phrases at the start of a sentence that add extra detail. We can use fronted adverbials to show how something has happened. We call these fronted adverbials of manner. Let's look at some examples... Quickly... Slowly... Lovingly... Dramatically... Using Fronted Adverbials to Show Why Fronted adverbials are words or phrases at the start of a sentence that add extra detail. We can use fronted adverbials to show why something has happened. We call these fronted adverbials of purpose. Let's look at some examples... To... To make money, Year Six started making slime. Because... Because I was hungry, I ate a sandwich. As... As she was tired, Katie stopped swimming. For... For the sake of his health, Richard went to the doctors. Using Fronted Adverbials to Show Why Fronted adverbials are words or phrases at the start of a sentence that add extra detail. We can use fronted adverbials to show why something has happened. We call these fronted adverbials of purpose. Let's look at some examples... As I am bored... Because I love you... Since I have a beard... Because my dog can drive...

resources.title: Saying How Often

content.topicNotes: Using Fronted Adverbials to Describe How Often Fronted adverbials are words or phrases at the start of a sentence that add extra detail. We can use fronted adverbials to describe how often something happens. We call these fronted adverbials of frequency. Let's look at some examples... Every... Every day, I walk my dog. Often... Often, I am late for school. Once... Once a week, I wash my hair. Twice... Twice a day, I brush my teeth.

resources.title: Saying Where & When

content.topicNotes: Using Fronted Adverbials for Describing Where Fronted adverbials are words or phrases at the start of a sentence that add extra detail. We can use fronted adverbials to show where something has happened. We call these fronted adverbials of place. Let's look at some examples... In... In the shed, Dad was hiding all the birthday presents for Jack. At... At the shopping centre, I bought new shoes. By... By the park, we met for our walk. Under... Under my bed, I found a teddy bear. Outside... Outside the greenhouse, I found a frog. Down... Down by the sea, they were holding a party. Examples of Fronted Adverbials Fronted adverbials are words or phrases at the start of a sentence that add extra detail. We can use fronted adverbials to show where something has happened. Here are some examples... Above the clouds Below the sea Upstairs Far away Using Fronted Adverbials to Describe When Fronted adverbials are words or phrases at the start of a sentence that add extra detail. We can use fronted adverbials to show when something has happened. We call these fronted adverbials of time. Let's look at some examples... At... At 3 o'clock, I will make a phone call. On... On Monday, I have a doctor's appointment. After... After lunch, I will go swimming. Before... Before school, I like to read my book. As soon as... As soon as she could, she rang her parents. Examples of Fronted Adverbials Fronted adverbials are words or phrases at the start of a sentence that add extra detail. We can use fronted adverbials to show when something has happened. Let's look at some examples... In the morning... At night... In the future... In winter... During summer...

resources.title: Scene & Seen

content.topicNotes: Scene and Seen Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings or spellings. Let's look at an example... Scene This is the scene of the crime. A scene is a place where something happens. A scene is also a part in a book or film where the action stays in the same place for a while. Seen After going to the cinema, she had seen the new film. If you have seen something, you have looked at it or watched it. Famous Film Scene This clip is from the famous restaurant scene in the Disney film Lady and the Tramp. The word 'scene' means a part of a film or book where the action stays in the same place for a while.

resources.title: Semi-Colon

content.topicNotes: Using Semi-Colons to Separate Clauses We don’t always need to use a full stop to separate main clauses. Sometimes we can use a semi-colon (;). Let's look at some examples... My boss is angry; I am late again It is cold; I hope it snows We are hungry; our lunch was tiny! I am so excited; I go on holiday next week I am scared; that snake is huge!

resources.title: Sentence Functions

content.topicNotes: The Function of Sentences The way a sentence is shaped tells you the function of the sentence. There are 4 main types or purposes of sentences: Questions Questions include asking about something or someone. Questions are really easy to spot because they end with a ‘?’. Questions must begin with a certain word, such as what, who, which, why, when, or where. Exclamations 1 There are 2 types of exclamatory sentences. One type of exclamatory sentence shows a sense of urgency, passion or anger in the voice. Sentences to show a sense of urgency, passion or anger in the voice end in a '!'. E.g. ‘I love this game!’, ‘Never eat cheese at night!’ and ‘I hate you!’ Exclamations 2 The other type of exclamation is when you begin with a question word (e.g. what, how, etc.), but you don’t ask a question. E.g. ‘What big ears you have!’ and ‘How lovely you look today!’ When you end a sentence with an exclamation mark, you don’t need another piece of punctuation. Statements Statements make up the bulk of our language. We use statements all the time. A statement is any sentence that is providing a fact, an opinion or a new piece of information. E.g. ‘John likes jelly’ is a statement providing us with new information about John. E.g. ‘Mary went to the shop’ also tells us something new about Mary. Commands Command sentences are called imperatives. Command sentences are used when you are insisting on someone doing something, or giving them an order. Commands examples The subject of the command sentence is always omitted, but it is implied that it is the second person ‘you’. ‘Get in the car’ is implying that 'you' should get in the car. ‘Stop that’ is implying that 'you' should stop that. If you wanted to add intensity to the expression, you would add the exclamation mark at the end of the command.

resources.title: Sentences
Shall

content.topicNotes: Shall Model verbs are verbs that affect other verbs in sentences. 'Shall' is a modal verb. Shall 'Shall' is used to show when something will definitely happen. Examples I shall have fun. You shall not cook. More examples Where shall we eat? He shall learn to read music.

resources.title: Shape & Place

content.topicNotes: Form - Shape Words containing 'form' generally relate to shape or form. Reform To reform is to change the form of something. Example: The rebels want political =reform=. Alternative: The rebels want political =change=. Conform To conform is to go along with the form or shape of something. Example: Many people in Germany =conformed= to the Nazi Party's mentality during World War II. Alternative: Many people in Germany =adopted= the Nazi Party's mentality during World War II. Form To form is to make something a specific shape. Example: According to the story of Genesis 2, God =formed= man from dust. Alternative: According to the story of Genesis 2, God =made= man from dust. Formation Words containing 'form' generally relate to shape. A formation can be the development of something into a certain shape. It can also be a particular arrangement. Doing something in formation means in a certain shape, pattern or structure. Loc - Place Words containing 'loc' are generally to do with place. Location A location is a place. Example: How far away is the =location=? Alternative: How far away is the =place=? Relocate To relocate is to move place. Example: Wilson =relocated= to the countryside. Alternative: Wilson =moved= to the countryside. Dislocate To dislocate is to move something out of place. Example: Harry =dislocated= his collarbone playing rugby. Alternative: Harry =injured= his collarbone playing rugby. Loc - Place Words containing 'loc' are generally to do with place. Here are some examples of words containing the root 'loc': Location Relocate Dislocate

content.topicNotes: Should Model verbs are verbs that affect other verbs in sentences. 'Should' is a modal verb. Should 'Should' is used to show something has to happen or is likely to happen.
